PRIVILEGE-MR. LACOMBE REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER ON JUNE 28
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. On June 28, 1943, the Prime Minister made the following statement in the house as reported at page 4072 of English Hansard:
The statement to which I refer is as follows:
"We have here in the cabinet three new millionaires who have made their money since the war's outbreak. We shall denounce them at the proper time and place. Fortunes are being built up."
The proper time and place to make a statement of that kind is in this House of Commons with the hon. member simultaneously undertaking to prove the charge or, if he is unable to do so, to resign his seat in this house. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member should be obliged either to withdraw the statement completely or else to convert it into a specific charge to be investigated in the usual manner, and the consequences of the investigation also to be followed up in the usual manner.
On my question of privilege I do say that those words which he then used about me bear a charge based upon an incorrect translar tion of the French debates of June 25 last. Because the Prime Minister did not verify the translation of the speech I gave in French I was subjected to serious wrong in respect of my privileges and prerogatives as a member of parliament. I was unfairly attacked by a certain portion of the press, and the incorrect translation of my speech, as quoted by the Prime Minister, was broadcast to all the country. This is the reason why, for the sake of truth, justice and honour, I ask the Prime Minister to withdraw the words which, on June 28 last, he unfairly said about me, on the basis of a highly incorrect translation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: VISIT OF CANADIAN MEMBERS TO WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand a copy of the Congressional Record, the proceedings and debates of the 78th congress, first session, Washington, Saturday, July 3, 
1943. This number contains an account of the visit made by members of congress to the meeting of the Empire Parliamentary Association at Ottawa. I understand that the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker), who was chairman of the conference, has also received a copy of the Congressional Record and would like to make reference to the visit of Canadian members to Washington arising out of what appears in the Congressional Record. If such is the case, I feel that my hon. friend might be permitted to make his remarks at this time.

subtopic: VISIT OF CANADIAN MEMBERS TO WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Prime Minister and the house for the opportunity of referring to the visit made by members of this house, together with the Speaker of the Senate, the Honourable Thomas Vien, to the Senate and the House of Representatives in Washington on June 30 and July 1.
The members of this house who were privileged to attend on that historic occasion were the hon. member for Stormont, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Chevrier), the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and myself. I think reference should be made to the kindness and the friendship and hospitality which were shown to us by both houses, not as individuals but as representatives of the parliaments of Canada and the other parts of the British empire. I need hardly say that the depth and warmth of their reception of us epitomized the devotion and the common sacrifices of the British empire and the United States of America in the present struggle, and it was the expressed hope and prayer of the members of congress, the members of the Canadian parliament, and of the parliaments of the United Kingdom, of Australia, of New Zealand and of Bermuda, that out of this meeting would come a repetition in the years to come of like meetings, and that the spirit of cooperation that now actuates the great democracies in the world should be continued in the days of peace.
I should mention the outstanding event of the visit which showed the appreciation of the United States of America of the empire as a whole, and of Canada, which was that for the first time in history, members of parliament from all parts of the empire were invited to take and did take desk seats on the floor of the United States Senate while it was in session. This was the greatest tribute that the United States Senate could pay to the representatives of the empire, and history was indeed made thereby on July 1, 1943. I hold in my hand a copy of the Congressional Record

Questions
of July 3, 1943, in which United States Senator Warren Austin, one of our distinguished visitors, referred to the visit of the representatives - of the United) States to Canada. Referring to the fact that delegations from all parts of the empire and the United States had attended, he said:
The subject of study and informal discussion [DOT]was the qualification and capacity of democracies to win the war and to attain peace that will prevail throughout the world.
The discussions were marked by eagerness for information, candour of expression and friendly understanding.
No obligations were sought or undertaken, but consequences of high value in mutual understanding were realized.
He goes on to say that with the unanimous consent of the Senate he would like to place upon the record the eloquent speeches made on the occasion of that visit by the Prime Minister of Canada, the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and the hon. member for Lethbridge. He used these words:
I concur in the opinion of the Prime Minister of Canada that "the resolution itself will in time become an historic document," and I believe that this first meeting of members of the Congress of the United States with members of the Empire Parliamentary Association is the beginning of a relationship among those bodies- which are closest to the people of the democracies-having endless possibilities of understanding and achievement.
He ends with these words:
The compliment of their visit to the Congress of the United States is further evidence of the intention of the democracies to cultivate a more perfect union for the prosecution of the war and the attainment of lasting peace.
The words of Senator Austin are reechoed by every hon. member of this house.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. ST. LAURENT: On June 30 the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen) asked a question on the orders of the day concerning the arrest of one Charles Brandel Crate. Perhaps I may be permitted to table the answer as if it were a question placed upon the order paper in the usual way.
Charles Brandel Crate is a former leader of the Canadian Union of Fascists. At the outbreak of the war he severed his connections with this organization and signed a statutory declaration to that effect.
The Canadian Union of Fascists was declared an illegal organization under the defence of Canada regulations in June, 1940, and there is no evidence that it had been functioning since, nor any attempts made to revive it.
Crate was engaged in August, 1942, by the Par Tex Foundation Company, Limited, Toronto, and was sent by this company to Newfoundland to work on a telephone construction line, which apparently the said company contracted to build. He returned to Canada in December, 1942.
In December, 1942, he obtained employment with the Dominion Bridge Company, Toronto, Ontario, as a labourer.
In January, 1943, he was engaged by the Don Construction Company and on the 28th of that month left for the company's camp at Dawson Creek, British Columbia. He worked there until about the end of May.
Crate arrived at Edmonton during the early part of June. He was arrested at Edmonton on June 21 and charged under section 39C of the defence of Canada regulations for having advocated the policies of an illegal organization, namely, the Canadian Union of Fascists. He appeared before Magistrate Miller on the 29th of June. No plea taken and accused remanded in custody until July
7.	The case is still before the courts.
Crate was employed in the area around Dawson Creek and did not go beyond that. This is not a restricted or prohibited area.
This man is a Canadian by birth, of English parentage, and as Dawson Creek is not in a restricted area he did not require a permit to travel to that area. It is understood that Crate has complied with the national selective service regulations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

Yes. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle asked the other night for the number of inspectors in the rural part of Saskatchewan. The member for New Westminster last night raised a question with regard to honey prices. Order 286 of the board, effective June 21, sets maximum prices to primary producers, on sales in bulk to processors or dealers, at 12$ cents or 14 cents for pasteurized. Primary producers may sell at retail to consumers at 15J cents in bulk when the purchaser provides his own container. In non-glass containers the maximum prices vary from 17J cents in 8-pound containers to 23 cents in one-pound containers; in glass, from 20$ cents in 4-pound jars to 35 cents in half-pound jars. The prices which I have given are for non-pasteurized, and for pasteurized, granulated, one must add 1$ cents per pound to all prices. It occurred to me that the hon. member said that the producers received before the war 20 cents per pound. That may have been in containers, and if so these prices would be consistent with that price.
There was also a question with regard to imported honey. All imported honey sold at retail must be sold strictly within the lawful price ceilings. During the autumn of 1942 and the winter of 1942-43 some imports of Mexican and Jamaican honey were authorized for sale to or use by industrial users, for example, packers and soft drink manufacturers, or by contractors operating construction or lumber camps. The cost to such users or contractors was in the majority of cases from 16 to 17 cents a pound. There were a few shipments where the laid-down cost to industrial users in Canada was in the neighbourhood of 20 cents. The board has no record of prices as high as 35 cents. In each case the industrial users were required to give an undertaking to absorb such increased costs of this raw material and not to raise their prices to their customers. During the past three months no new authorizations for the sale of imported honey at higher than ceiling prices have been given, even to industrial users. It is however lawful for an industrial user to purchase honey in a foreign country and bring it into Canada for his own use, since no purchase or sale takes place in Canada.
The member for Lake Centre asked for the record of the percentage or proportion of recommendations of regional counsel which were acted upon. The records of the enforcement administration are not kept in such form as to make readily available the number of prosecutions recommended by the regional offices. A careful estimate however indicates that approximately 75 per cent of such recommendations are approved by head office in Ottawa. The percentage varies of course as between the several regions-as low as 60

or 65 per cent in some and as high as 90 per cent in others. Those are the main points.
Do I understand the minister to say that only a percentage of the prosecutions were authorized by the head office?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. All that take place are. What I have been saying is that recommendations are received from regional counsel which in some cases are not accepted by the head office.
Does the chairman of the board authorize the prosecutions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The wartime prices and trade board?
Does the chairman of the wartime prices board issue the authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The board itself as such does so.

There has been
considerable publicity and talk about black markets in Canada, especially in meat. I have heard that there has been a great deal of interference from packing bouses, either by telephone or otherwise, and it has been said that certain threats were made over the telephone by the heads of certain packing houses to the chairman of the prices and trade board. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certain threats?
In some cases. That is what I am informed. Just what interference has there been from officials of packing houses with the chairman of the prices board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no knowledge whatever of any threats to the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, coming from anyone.
There has been no attempt at all at interference by officials of packing houses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not so far as I know. The official of the board who would be in a position to know says that he knows of none.
I do not think the minister has answered1 all the questions I asked. For example, there was a question as to the division between various types of prosecutions, rental and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I gave that last night.

Oh; they were
given?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board

I have here a most
important document, a return I first secured showing that for the first three years of operations of the wartime prices and trade board, down to June 15, 1942-three years less two months-the number of prosecutions has been 150. In this connection I have a return to an order of the house with regard to the enforcement of the law. This is sessional paper No. 341, Monday, June 29, 1942. I will read the questions:
1.	How many people, by provinces, have been prosecuted in the law courts for not carrying out the orders in council and instructions, rules and regulations and directions of various boards and controllers and dollar-a-year men, including the wartime prices and trade board, and various non-legislative bodies?
2.	What lawyers, by provinces, have been retained, and what are their fees?
3.	Does the Department of Justice provide counsel to enforce federal law for the wartime prices and trade board and other federal boards?
In reply to the first question the answer is:
1. Numbers of persons prosecuted for alleged contraventions of regulations, orders and requirements of the wartime prices and trade board, September 3, 1939, to June 15, 1942:
Nova Scotia	 8
New Brunswick	 1
Quebec	 22
Ontario	 96
Manitoba	 6
Saskatchewan	 8
British Columbia	 9
In reply to the third question, whether the Department of Justice provide counsel to enforce federal law for the wartime prices and trade board and other federal boards, the answer is yes. The minister said that there have been 150 prosecutions in two years and ten and a half months.
Last night the minister announced that of 3,335 prosecutions from December 1, 1941, to May 31, 1943, 894 were for infractions of price rules, 952 rentals, 465 rationing and 225 sundries, like gasoline. I can tell you that in the city of Toronto the fines levied in connection with many of these prosecutions are not uniform. The magistrates impose heavy fines; the people are not given time in which to pay, and they have to go to gaol. There should be a standard of action and uniform enforcement in these cases; and in any case why should we in Toronto have the greatest number of these rental prosecutions, while the prosecutions in connection with rationing, gasoline and so on, amounted to only some 465? Then where are these people detained? We
know that during the depression the government of Canada, in order to relieve unemployment, built many municipal institutions all across Canada, though Ontario did not get any. In some of the provinces they built gaols, schools, court houses and places of that kind, thus relieving the local taxpayers. In the county of York they have a gaol which was built shortly after confederation and which does not provide adequate accommodation for these people. As a result there is a good deal of suffering. I believe the minister is very humane and I suggest that he should look into these matters and consult with the enforcement officers as to equality of treatment and more reasonable fines for petty breaches.
Then I should like to know why a number of these young solicitors are employed in enforcement work when they should be doing war service. I have noticed some of the names in the newspapers, and I cannot understand why the Department of Justice should engage these young prosecutors when there are crown attorneys in all the districts whose duty it is to enforce the federal laws. The enforcement of all federal laws comes under the provincial attorneys general and their deputies, the crown attorneys in the police courts throughout the country. I do not know why these other solicitors should be engaged.
I appreciate what has been done by the minister in freezing rents in order to protect the poor people, especially in the cities. He has done very good work, but I believe the time has come when we should have a vast housing policy, because under present conditions no one wants to own property. The minister has a parliamentary secretary, one of whose relatives was for a number of years our corporation counsel. I refer to the late Mr. W. C, Chisholm, K.C., a very capable official, who went into this enforcement matter thoroughly some years ago. At that time it was found that a large share of the work of enforcing federal statutes was carried on by the police departments and crown attorneys of the various cities, who had that much less time in which to carry on their other duties. I do believe the municipalities should be given some help in this enforcement work. I believe some contribution is made in connection with the detention costs, but then I believe there is altogether too much detention. Many of those offences are merely trivial; many people are brought to court unnecessarily, though where serious offences occur of course there should be proper punishment. We should never legislate against human nature, but I am sure the minister and his assistant have done very good work.

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board

I am sure all the members of this committee sympathize with the minister and the officials of the wartime prices and trade board in the very difficult and responsible duties they have to perform. I noticed that Canada's first minister of finance brought down in this house in 1867 a budget with expenditures during the first five months of just a little over $5,000,000, and that the monthly expenditures at that time were less than we are spending in two hours now. The controls necessary in order that the burdens of modern warfare may be distributed fairly and evenly across the country are very complicated. I think the minister and his staff are to be congratulated on having been able to bring the public of Canada along with them so well and to have so few black markets and so few people in various parts of the country who are trying to take advantage of the regulations. I have a letter from the chairman of one of the war finance committees in my constituency in which he states that his district raised $42,000 though the quota was only $28,000 in the last campaign. In his letter he went on to say:
We have very little canvassing to do this time, as it was great the way the people came in with their subscriptions. One party had twenty-nine cream cheques saved up. Several people of very little means came in and bought on the instalment plan. Those are the kind that give a canvasser more pep. Those are the ones that we fight to save.
That is from a veteran of the last war, writing as chairman of the committee, and I think it important that we maintain this attitude right across the country.
Before I discuss the two questions I want to bring to the attention of the minister I might say that planning by people who are opposed to social planning has produced some worth while results. One of the press releases referring to order A-314 of the wartime prices and trade board states that the order has had the effect of eliminating at least one hundred million truck miles per annum, which is said to be an ultra conservative figure, with few instances in which justifiable criticism based on actual hardship could be levelled at the board, either because of lack of service or increased cost. Then it goes on to say that in the ice cream industry in Ontario between 60 and 70 per cent of the mileage previously run has been saved, at an actual dollar and cents saving to the industry. In other words, competition in the industry had in peace time wasted from 60 to 70 per cent of delivery costs, and since we have demonstrated that this wastage can be avoided in war time I hope we may have similar controls when the war is over, for the greatest good to the greatest, number.
'-Mr- Church.]
The minister's parliamentary assistant brought down for me some answers in connection with the amount of sugar being made available this year for canning, for the soft drink industry, for the manufacture of wines, and for the making of candy. I should like the minister to regard himself as the father of a very large family-the people of Canada- with the welfare of that family to consider. This year he is providing about ten pounds of sugar per person for canning. At the same time, according to these figures, he is providing 6-6 pounds of sugar per person for the making of soft drinks, -9 pound per person for the making of wines, and 4-8 pounds for the making of candy. The actual figures as they were brought down in the house are 66,000,000 pounds for soft drinks, 9,100,000 pounds for wines, 48,000,000 pounds for candy and 100,000,000 pounds for preserving. To work it out on the actual amount of sugar available for the minister's family this year, on the assumption that he has three children-I do not think that is correct, but assuming that he has the average family he would receive ten pounds of sugar for each person, or a total of fifty pounds of sugar for canning purposes. He would have thirty-three pounds for making soft drinks, four and a half pounds for making wine, and twenty-four pounds for making candy. I suggest that the minister and his assistant discuss this matter in their family circles to-night, and note the reaction of the members of their families.
I understand the difficulties. I know that the soft drink industry in Canada has a large investment. I know that less sugar is available to them than was available last year. But the information we have seems to indicate that they have far too much sugar made available,	taking into consideration the
amounts provided for essential purposes such as canning and preserving.
I received only this morning a communication from the sugar protest committee of Victoria, British Columbia, a communication which I believe other hon. members also have received. People across Canada are not organized; they cannot make their protests vocally. But I believe there is a genuine protest across Canada against giving a family of five only fifty pounds for canning, and at the same time giving them thirty-three pounds for soft drinks, four and a half pounds for wine, and twenty-four pounds for candy.
I realize that some educational work must be done immediately to counteract the influence of the people who make soft drinks available. I have been disturbed by the reply made in confectionery stores when requests have been made for soft drinks, when none

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
were available. They say, "'Blame Mr. Usley lor this", instead of "'Blame Hitler". I suggest that the wartime information board should be trying to have our people understand that we cannot have suggar for canning and for our children if we are going to continue to make this very large volume of sugar available for the soft drinks industry.
And the wine industry.

Certain hon. members may think I am a crank on the question of drink. I think in peace time the soft drink industry provides an alternative to harder liquors. But with the tremendous amount of fruit which will waste this year there will have to be some change in the amount of sugar made available.
In connection with trucking I would point out that I placed a question on the order paper in which I asked how many trucks in Canada delivering soft drinks exclusively have been permitted to operate beyond the thirty-five mile limit. The answer to that was 222. Then I asked how many trucks delivering beer exclusively operated beyond the thirty-five mile limit, and the answer was 203. To the question as to how many trucks belonging to wholesale produce dealers were permitted to operate beyond the thirty-five mile limit, the answer was 126.
In my constituency we have a large wholesale produce industry. That industry has large territories to cover, in which only a poor train service operates. They are placing on the market a very large volume of eggs for purposes of processing for the British trade. My information is that they have not been able to obtain permission to operate beyond the thirty-five mile area. At the same time soft drink trucks go whizzing by, and apparently they have no difficulty at all in securing adequate supplies of both gasoline and rubber. I submit we are allowing the soft drink industry two great concessions. I would ask the minister to make a statement indicating whether something can be done this year to make more sugar available for canning and less available for soft drinks and wine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I should discuss one at a time the purposes for which sugar is made available. The cut in the amount of sugar made available for candy is thirty per cent this year below the amount allowed in 1941. The same cut of thirty per cent is made in respect of wine and soft drinks. The hon. member says that the relationship of the amount used for these purposes to the amount available for canning of fruit is an incorrect relationship. To begin with I would point out that the thirty per cent cut is a substantial
and severe one. The hon. member seems to think that we should discourage to a greater extent than we do the use of soft drinks. Well, human beings are so constituted, whether we like it or not, that they have to drink something.
What about cold water?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Legislative bodies which have tried to decree that the only drink should be cold water have encountered some little resistance in public opinion. And if they are to have freedom to drink something other than water, I suppose the alternatives are soft drinks and beer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Oh no-milk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a food rather than a drink.
And buttermilk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The possibility of utilizing these food drinks-because that is what they are-in a large way, is limited. I know the hon. member does not think that people should drink more beer. And with a very large number of persons in the country complaining that they cannot get as much beer as they would like, I am afraid that the discontent of the population would be considerable if we made an extremely drastic cut in the amount of soft drinks they can obtain. We are told that in war plants the availability of soft drinks is essential to morale. It would not be essential to my morale, and probably not to the morale of my hon. friend; but it does appear that there are a great many people in the country who do like to drink some soft drinks. I am afraid that if we cut the amount of soft drinks by more than thirty per cent, along with the cut in beer which has taken place, we would have a greater outcry than we should have in a time of war.
With regard to candy I would direct the minds of hon. members back to a session or two ago when we were discussing the thirty per cent tax on candy. I well recall the speeches made at that time. I remember speeches by hon. members who are also members of the medical profession, in which they argued that candy was not an article we should tax, because it was a good energy-producing food, particularly for children. We all remember the story about those poor little boys and girls who, we were told, were going into the stores to buy a stick of candy for a cent. They would reach up their little hands and hold out the cent to the storekeeper, saying, "A cent's worthy of candy, please", and the storekeeper would say, "Oh, no, my child; that is two cents now, because of the Mackenzie King government." I think it was
4436	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
the hon. member for Peterborough West who accused us of having arranged it so that we would even take candy from kids. I am just mentioning these things to show that candy has made friends-or at least that it had a lot of friends at that time in the House of Commons. If we cut down to too great an extent the amount of sugar available for candy we get results which are not the results we should like to have.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister must have been more impressed than we thought he was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, I was touched by the speech of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: So were the taxpayers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is what the hon. member said. With regard to wine, we are following the same course; that is subject to a thirty per cent cut. The hon. gentleman referred to the heavy investment, and the implication was that we were very tender toward heavy investors. Whenever anything is done about wine the investors who are most vocal are the grape growers. They are the ones who protest most vociferously when anything is done which unduly affects wine. Nevertheless we have passed an order in council which prohibits wines being reinforced by spirits, and we are subjecting them to the same type and degree of sugar control as applies to other industries. Here again I think the only proper policy is not to go to extremes.
The hon. gentleman says that much fruit will be wasted, but the reports I get are that the fruit crop is very light in Canada, that in many cases it is going to be difficult to get fruit. Some people will have more sugar than they will be able to use, and! some will have less, possibly a great deal less, than they will be able to use. So far as I have been able to ascertain, the people of Canada never used more than 100,000,000 pounds of sugar for the canning of fruit. In 1942, when they were given the privilege of securing as much sugar as they requested for canning purposes, they required only 106,000,000 pounds. That represents practically one hundred per cent as against the seventy per cent being supplied to these other industries. If the hon. gentleman can work out a more rational policy than the one we are following, I should be glad to have him do it. The hon. gentleman mentioned beer and soft drink trucks.
And wholesale produce trucks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should like to delay answering that until I have looked over a memorandum which has been placed before me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As the question of sugar rationing has been reintroduced into the discussion, there are one or two matters I should like to bring up. Will the minister clarify the position in connection with the international sugar board? The information I have-perhaps the minister will correct me if it is erroneous -is that the amount which can be had for this purpose is regulated by an international sugar board which operates not only so far as Canada is concerned but with respect to the United States. I note from an article which appeared in a Fairfield, Maine, newspaper that the amount of sugar being provided for canning in Maine is twenty-five pounds maximum. That is a maximum, not an arbitrary or a minimum amount. As I read the article, it states that a top limit of twenty-five pounds of sugar per person was set under new regulations which became effective on May 15.
If there is an international sugar board or any arrangement which covers both countries, we ought to be entitled to as much for. canning purposes as is allowed in the United States. It is natural that thoughts of discrimination will arise, particularly along the border. This is one point I should like the minister to clear up. While I am on my feet I should like to place a letter on the record on behalf of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling), who has asked me to do this for him. He is very much interested in this matter. He received a copy of a letter addressed from Silverton, British Columbia, to the ration administrator, Confederation building, Montreal, Quebec, under date of June 25, 1943. It reads as follows:
We have to-day received from the Nelson, British Columbia, ration committee, coupons for sugar for canning, amounting to thirty pounds for our family of three.
It was understood that rural districts where fruit is extensively grown in gardens, would receive at least fifteen pounds per person.
This ration allotted us amounts to one crate of fruit per person for the entire season's canning, and no sugar for jam. This is a ridiculous allotment, in view of the fact that it has been impossible to secure any supplies of jams, jellies, or canned fruit through retail channels in this district, and also in view of the fact that in practically every home, raspberries, strawberries, cherries and currants have been given extensive cultivation in preparation for the season when home canning and jam making would have to take the place of bought goods.
Those of us with small patches of berries and fruits might just as well cut them down, as the crops will now go to waste, and this in a country which is in a state of war.
According to press reports British Columbia, a fruit producing area, has been given the lowest allotment per person in Canada. Why?
Last year, according to official statistics, the amount of sugar used for home canning and

War Appropriation-
-Finance-
-Prices Board
preserving was about as much as the allotment for 1943. Yet everyone who did home canning had ample. Why are we cut to one crate of small fruit per person this year? If eight and a half million people have applied for sugar for canning, there is something wrong in the administration of the sugar distribution. After many years in the wholesale fruit business, I am convinced that there is no such thing as 85 per cent of the population of Canada preserving at home. Fifty per cent would be a high figure. Either your figures are inaccurate or else almost 50 per cent of those applying have no intention of using this sugar for canning, thereby cutting the allotment for those who legitimately intend doing so.
Your figures in your circular are also out of line. You claim there are 100,000,000 pounds sugar available for canning among eight and a half million applications.
According to my way of figuring, this would work out to almost 12 pounds per person. Why only 10 pounds in a fruit producing district?
If the same amount was used in preserving last year, then only 5,000,000 people used preserving sugar, including men, women and children, as the amount used was about 20 pounds per person on the average. Where have the three and a half million extra users of sugar come from? An increase of 70 per cent?
On what basis has this distribution been made that some districts, non-fruit producing, receive more than those which produce fruit in the home yards?
What information and from what source was it gathered upon which the distribution was made? What steps have been, or will be taken to ensure that the allotment given will be used for preserving? (It would take an army of policemen to check each individual's canning operations.)
As citizens who are making sacrifices to enable this war to be fought to a successful conclusion, we have the right to ask pertinent questions, which affect the distribution of the sacrifice, and sugar for our families on an equitable basis.
It has been proved conclusively on several occasions so far since the war started that administration for the whole of Canada cannot be done effectively from points w-hich are over 3,000 miles from the area administered, and possibly this is the answer to some of the questions which the people of British Columbia are asking.
I want to thank the minister and the house for permitting me to read this letter on behalf of the member for Kootenay West, who had asked me to do so when this item was under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for York-Sunbury raised the question of the use of sugar in the United States as compared with Canada in the house on June 4, and instead of replying in the house I wrote him on June 17-
Mr. GRAYD'ON: Did he make the same suggestion as is made here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, he did not give this figure. He raised the question because he said the restaurants of the United States
seemed to be a little freer with their sugar than restaurants here. Perhaps I had better read the letter I wrote to him:
Dear Mr. Hanson:
Ou June 4 you asked me in the house for information as to the allocation of sugar supplies for Canada as compared with the United States.
At the end of 1941 it became obvious that the United States and Canada would have to ration sugar due to the shortage of ships to carry sufficient raw sugar from producing areas to the United States and Canada.
At that time, many discussions w-ere held in Washington between the Sugar Administration and the office of Price Administration and other competent American government agencies. Subsequently, the ration administration was formed and participated in these discussions.
It was laid down as a principle between the Canadian and United States government agencies that as far as possible the two ration schemes should be as nearly equal as local geographical, economic and distributive conditions permitted. At the present time, the per capita consumption, excluding the needs of the army, is almost exactly the same, being about 66 pounds per head in the United States and 65 pounds per head in Canada. This consumption of 65. pounds per head is the total amount of sugar consumed in Canada for household, home canning, industrial and institutional use, divided by the population.
At the beginning of rationing, the sugar administration felt that the restaurant business, in order to save sugar, would require to be authorized to remove sugar bowls, from the table. If this -was not made mandatory, competitors might have nullified any saving in restaurant consumption. In the United States, such removal of sugar bowls has not been made mandatory but a very large number of restaurants and hotels only serve one tablet of sugar for a beverage and a little envelope of soft sugar for cereal or fruit. The envelope contains less than one teaspoonful and one tablet is less than three lumps. From our investigation and experience, the amount of sugar allowed to clients in restaurants in United States is appreciably less than in Canada, although there are exceptions where it is possible, on demand, to obtain more.
The allocation of sugar internationally is made by the combined food board through its sugar committee, on which Canada is represented. At meetings of this committee, Canada, United States and Great Britain present figures of their requirements and available supplies are allocated in accordance with relative need. Canada and the United States share on a similar basis, our ration plans being almost identical. The United Kingdom is slightly differently placed, in that larger stocks have to be carried and disseminated throughout the island for security reasons.
We are dependent upon the United States for our share of raw sugar to the extent of about one-third, in that the war shipping administration has given the Canadian sugar administration an undertaking to lift in 1943, 100,000 tons of raw sugar by American flag vessels. United States government agencies, therefore, expect to be assured that we are not providing more sugar per capita in Canada than they are themselves in the United States.
4438	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
I have no definite information as to how they have divided their sugar in the United States between canning and ordinary purposes. The officials tell me that it is their opinion, although they do not vouch for this, that one billion pounds of sugar has been allocated by the United States for home canning, which would be a smaller amount per capita than in Canada, and their information also is that the amount allowed in the United States is 25 pounds per family rather than per person. But I am not in a position to deny -what the hon. gentleman has said.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Just to have the matter made clear perhaps I might read into the record this one paragraph for the minister to check, because it raises a question which it seems to me will have to be decided one way or the other. This article appeared in the Fairfield Review, in Maine, on May 15 last. It is entitled "Canning Sugar", and reads:
Procedure by which housewives will obtain sugar for home canning and freezing of this season's fruit crop on and after May 15 was released Monday by the Maine district office ot price administration. As previously announced by price administrator Prentiss M. Brown, sugar for home canning is being allotted on substantially the same basis as last year, that is, one pound for each four quarts (or eight pounds) of the finished product, and by essentially the same procedure-written application to the local board. A top limit-
I spoke of that before as being a mistake.
A top limit of 25 pounds of sugar per person Isse^ *n new regulations, which become effective May 15^ The OPA emphasizes, however, that the 25-pound figure is a maximum, to be granted only in the relatively few cases where this large amount of fruit will be canned and preserved. Last year there was no nationwide ceiling over the amount that was allowed each person, but many local boards set individual limits of 10 or 15 pounds, while others granted individual amounts as high as 45 pounds. The new limit of 25 pounds per person assures more uniform treatment, although it is not expected that many families will apply for the maximum amount. Within the 25-pound per person limit, any family can apply for sugar to put up jams, jellies and preserves at the rate of five pounds per individual. This is a more generous allowance than last year, when sugar for preserves was limited to one pound per person.
I leave that with the minister, so that the whole record will be clear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before we go any
further I should like to refer to the statement made by the leader of the opposition. This sugar discussion has been taking place on several occasions. It is an important question,
[Mr. Ilsley.)
and perhaps it would suit the convenience of hon. members and the minister if we disposed of the sugar question first.

The minister referred to the curtailment which is to take place in various lines of production, but he did not say anything with regard to a curtailment in the consumption of sugar permitted for the commercial canning of fruits and for the making of jam.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no limit for commercial canning.
Or for making jam?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Or for jam making, no.
There would be a limit on account of other factors, such as the amount of fruit available; but they can get the sugar that is required.
There is a cut of thirty per cent in sugar for use in the making of soft drinks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
But the cut to the housewife who does her own canning is a great deal worse than thirty per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no cut below last
year.
The canning factories have to use a thin syrup; they are not allowed to use a heavy syrup-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They have to use a thin
syrup.
That is their cut?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I think it is realized by the people of Canada that the difficulties we are experiencing because of the rationing of sugar arise out of the sheer stupidity of the men who have been in charge of this country for the last six years. I can support my stand very easily. There is no reason in the world why Canada should not be producing all the sugar that Canada needs.
Absolutely none.

As far back as 1936 I began to draw to the attention of hon. members the danger we were running into by reason of a war restricting the amount of sugar which could be brought into this country. Generally speaking, whenever I made such a remark some of the wise men on the Liberal side passed my warnings off

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
very lightly. Oh, they were buoyant in, their disregard in those dlays. Now we see the country in the difficulties which their buoyancy and simple-mindedness have run us into. I wish to point out that there was plenty of time in 1936 to have made provision for all the sugar which Canada would need, and anyone with real intelligence and the disposition to use it could have seen at that time that there was serious danger of a war. I rose in this chamber in 1937, and again in 1938 and 1939, and I pleaded with hon. members and with the government to increase sugar production in Canada. Not a word was said in reply

not one. In 1941 I had to rise in my place and devote a considerable amount of attention to the problem of sugar, because it was proposed by some all-wise individual in Canada that we restrict by 1.300 acres the amount of sugar beets which could be planted in the southern Alberta area.
Surely not restrict the production?
Yes. It was only after a great deal of effort that certain stupid men could be brought to see that such restriction was really wrong and that the 1,300 acres should be permitted to be grown.

Are the farmers of
southern, Alberta actually prevented from raising all the sugar beets they wish to raise?

Oh, undoubtedly. The hon. member will find in Hansard of April 3, 1941, my speech dealing with the whole question, if he is interested enough to look it up. That was actually proposed in Canada, and but for a good deal more effort than should have been necessary it would have been adopted.
I believe it is time that we as members of the house and the people generally in Canada should begin to recognize that it is a good thing for a country to be producing what it needs. Generally speaking, people admire the mixed farmer; they generally rejoice over a mixed farming area, and those areas as a rule are more stable than one-crop areas. Now, Canada is far from stable economically. But we are in a position now to start over again. At least we can begin to start to plan over again. I hope that by some means we can manage to prevent the people who have charge of the planning policies of this country from developing such fatuous ideas about the national economy as have prevailed since 1935, such ideas as that we ought to specialize in one, or two, or three
or more commodities and import just as much as we possibly can, so that we can export. Why were we supposed to restrict our sugar production in this country? Why? So that we could sell salt fish to Cuba. It sounds most attractive now, does it not,- salt fish and potatoes to Cuba? And in order to be able to sell salt fish and potatoes, we were to restrict the development of the beet sugar industry in Canada. If you can imagine anything that looks more stupid in the light of what has happened since, come around and tell me about it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Unless you happen to be catching fish.

I wish to point out furthermore that it was possible for us to have brought into Canada in the spring of 1941 two big beet sugar factories. They would have been producing sugar in the fall of 1941. There are areas in the province of Alberta in which those factories could have been established, and sugar would have been coming on to the market greatly to the relief of the sugar situation in Canada. Now it may seem impossible for hon. members to believe this, but I personally went to members of the government and urged upon them the advisability and the necessity of allowing those two factories to come into Canada and of setting up conditions and circumstances which would assure them of getting a market if they did come in; but I was met with a courteous disregard. Not only that: in the spring of 1942 we could have had another factory, but the government let it go. I wonder how long the people of this country and the members of this house are going to submit to a management of the country's affairs so open to question as this kind of thing is.
I thought it was fitting, Mr. Chairman, that we should do a lot of thinking about this matter before we left the subject of sugar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, at the risk of enhancing my reputation for stupidity I should like to point out two or three qualifications of the hon. gentleman's remarks. I do not think anyone ever suggested that Canada should or could put herself in a position to supply all her requirements from beet sugar production in Canada.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Because the economic sacrifice involved in so doing would be too great. The opportunity for expansion is not there, except at a tremendous cost. At the present time, or before the war, if I remember correctly, the total proportion of sugar derived

4440	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
from sugar beets in Canada was about 15 per cent, and it rose to about 18 per cent. Of course there is a vast difference between that and 100 per cent; and certainly I never heard it suggested by the hon. gentleman or anyone else that it was feasible to fill that gap between 18 and 100 per cent. Those who have advocated a subsidized -and greatly expanded programme of sugar beet production in Canada have been ambitious to get it up to a little higher figure; that is all. If that all along has been the only policy which would be arguably sound, I think the hon. gentleman's assertion that if we had been supplying a larger part of our requirements from beet sugar production we would have had more sugar for use by the civilian population is incorrect, because the amount of sugar we are able to get from abroad takes into account the amount of sugar which is available in Canada, and if we were to double our beet sugar production in this country we would be denied a proportionate amount of cane sugar by way of importation. So that the results of the ineptitude of ministers and governments and so on, if such it were, are not the results which the hon. gentleman has portrayed so feelingly. It would not have meant that we would have had more sugar; it would merely have meant that a larger proportion of the same amount of sugar would have been grown here instead of being imported.
I think the minister ought to explain the statement he made that it would be impossible except at very great cost to produce Canadian sugar in Canada. Before he starts to meet my contention-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not intend to start.
Then he has made a statement which is utterly unsupported and unsupportable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

Yes, sir; utterly
unsupported and unsupportable. I doubt if there is a province in Canada in which a sugar factory could not be established.

We have them in
Ontario.

Certainly they could be established in Ontario to supply all Ontario's needs, and certainly in Manitoba; and in the Carrot River valley in Saskatchewan I am told the same could be done. In Alberta fifteen factories could be operated, each of which would supply five per cent of Canada's total needs. I am positive that a sugar factory could be established in British Columbia, and I have had representations 
from Nova Scotia to the effect that they could establish one successfully there. Under the circumstances, I wonder how the minister can support his claim that it would be too costly. Let me give him another thought before he attempts this task, which he may rush into, because he has got into the habit of recklessness in the matter of sugar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why were they not established?

Because sufficient
encouragement was not given.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Who would pay for the encouragement?
The encouragement could be paid for very easily.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By whom?

I happen to come from an area where sugar is produced and I know a few things about sugar. All the minister has to know is this-and I have already pointed this out to the house! In the Raymond area, where I was living when I was elected, the sugar factory sold its sugar at just about four cents per pound in 1937 to the wholesaler. That is so cheap that the prospect of buying sugar at four cents per pound must appear to the people of Canada as utopian. They sold their sugar at four cents a pound and the factory made $155 an acre gross for every acre that was used in the production of sugar beets. If that is not enough to show that sugar can be produced economically in Canada, there must be something that I have overlooked, and I do not think there is. All that would have been necessary would have been to-guarantee to the producers of sugar beets-access to the Canadian market first. That is all. As matters were, it was so easy for the Department of Finance or the department of inland revenue to change a certain duty ever so little, and thereby admit sugar from cane producing areas at an exceedingly lower rate to destroy the beet sugar production enterprise here. A great many people-had to abandon the idea of going in for the production of beet sugar, which otherwise they would have undertaken.
I think it would have been found that the economic advantage to Canada which would have accrued from the raising of our own. sugar beets and the production of our own. sugar would have been so great that it would have doubly compensated us for any possible-expenditure which we might have had to make as a government to protect the beet sugar-industry.

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
Let me give one example. A 1200-ton slicing capacity mill at Raymond in my constituency is estimated by responsible American authorities to be capable of keeping 10,000 people; not only those who grow the beets and those who process them in the factory, but those who produce the coal and the various other items that contribute to that processing, those who haul the beets, those who care for them, those who take care of the live stock which are produced in a beet sugar area because of the abundance of feed there; hay grown in the crop rotation in preparation for the beets; beet pulp, beet tops, beetalasses, and so on. When all these factors are taken into consideration it will be seen that a 1200-ton slicing capacity mill will keep 10,000 people. We were keeping people on relief in Canada year after year and paying for it out of the dominion treasury as well as out of provincial and municipal treasuries. That is one simple example. Moreover, we were losing all the revenues that would have gone to the railways for the hauling of the beets and the hauling of the sugar and all that sort of thing.
Even these two considerations will constitute a serious obstacle for the minister to climb over in establishing his contention that Canada could not on economic grounds afford to have produced her own sugar.
Let me make one more observation before I resume my seat. We have been hearing a good deal lately about the food conference at Hot Springs, Virginia. The most important pronouncement that came out of that conference was that never yet had mankind produced enough food. They omitted, I grant, to say something else of equal importance, if not indeed of greater importance, namely, that never had mankind been able to pay for the food that it had been able to produce. They did say, however, that mankind had never produced enough food, and they urged that every means be taken to increase the food production of the world in every country. If their advice means anything at all it should mean that in Canada we should increase our food production, and among the foods which should receive first consideration, apart from commodities which we now produce in abundance, such as wheat and other grains and vegetables, beet sugar should be prominent.

I should not like the remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge to pass without in a measure agreeing *with his general premise, but I am more particularly anxious to emphasize, or at any rate to confirm, the view which the hon. member took back in 1936, that our country should see to it, in the interests of the generations that will 72537-2814
come after us, that in the supply of all necessary commodities, and particularly foodstuffs, for every individual commodity we should at least have some source of supply, even though that source might be very limited in comparison with requirements. . At any rate, our country, Canada, should have a spot where that particular commodity might be produced,, and I say that Alberta is such a spot for sugar.
I rise now merely to emphasize the hon. member's remarks. Coming from the central province of Ontario, I commend to the consideration of the house his remarks of 1936-and his consistent and continued argument: from that day forward, because, in common with members from Alberta, I would point out that in western Ontario at Wallaceburg, and in the counties of Essex and Kent and through that area, we are able to produce a certain amount of this particular commodity. The economics of production is another matter. If we had a world-wide free interchange of all commodities the situation would be different. It is perhaps not feasible or economically possible to produce our own requirements in certain lines within the confines of our own country. It is probably true that sugar can be-produced more easily and more economically in the West Indies and other areas closer to-the equator than it can be produced here; but if future events should once more give people the disposition to become more self-sufficient than is the case at present we may be forced' into the position of keeping lit the embers of the fire which made it possible for us to-begin the production, within the confines of.' our own country, of a very necessary commodity such as sugar. I believe the hon. member for Lethbridge deserves the commendation of this house for the effort he has put forward, ever since he has been a member of this chamber, in keeping to the fore the possibility of Canada producing her own sugar requirements. It is true, as the Minister of Finance has said, that our own production amounts to only fifteen per cent of our consumption at the present time, but still that fifteen per cent might sustain us should the world economic position become so desperate that we would have to depend upon Alberta or Ontario for our sugar requirements. But apart from the economies of the situation there is the fact that 10,000 people can be sustained by this industry within our own country.
That is by just one factory.

As the hon. member says, that is in connection with only one factory; and before we are very much older
4442	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
the day may come when we shall be happy to find employment for 10,000 of our citizens, whether in Alberta or in Ontario. Further than that, we must keep our transportation system going, and any little help it may get from the sugar industry in connection with transportation from Alberta to the consuming centres of Ontario and Quebec might help out very considerably.
I am very anxious, as I am sure the Minister of Finance is anxious, that the observations of the hon. member for Lethbridge should be borne in mind in the days to come, so that we may give some thought and study to the development of another necessary industry within our borders, not only to keep our own people employed, not only to maintain a balanced national economic system, but also in order that those of our people who desire to exercise their talents in this particular branch of industry may have an opportunity to do so. We must produce sugar for our own needs; and while it is true that the larger part of that sugar comes from other parts of the world, I believe we should maintain some production in Canada. The efforts of the hon. member for Lethbridge in connection with the production of sugar in Canada have been really worth while. I believe they will find a ready echo in the western part of Ontario, particularly in the counties of Essex and Kent, and more particularly in the town of Wallaeeburg, whose refineries have been idle oftener than they should have been; as well as in the city of Chatham.

I
think I should keep the record straight and talk about the sugar industry for a moment or two, since the question has been discussed at some length by the hon. member for Lethbridge and the hon. member for Dan-forth. It does seem to me that we should settle once and for all whether or not it is economically sound to produce our own sugar in Canada; for this question has been bandied around the house ever since I came here, in 1935, and for many years before that. Neither this nor any other government of Canada has given much encouragement to the production of sugar beets in Canada, though I have no doubt that from an economic point of view, we cannot compete with the sugar cane industry of the West Indies, Cuba or some of the other southern islands, so far as price is concerned.
The previous speaker mentioned the counties of Essex, Kent and Lambton, and referred to the sugar refineries in that area. It is true that we have two modern sugar refineries .there, capable of processing approximately

40,000 acres of beets annually. This year, in spite of all the efforts that have been put forth, only about 10,000 acres of beets, or perhaps less, are being grown. If another 30,000 acres were produced we would be able to produce approximately 75,000,000 pounds more sugar in Canada.

May I ask why that is
not being produced?

I was just coming to that. The contract that has been offered to the growers is very good, probably fifteen or eighteen per cent better than last year, but there are several factors entering into it. From the point of view of returns, sugar beets must compete with such crops as corn, soya beans, white beans and so on, which probably would not give an equal gross return, but which probably give an equal net return. The question of labour also enters into the problem. It is difficult to guarantee sufficient labour to stimulate the production of this additional 30,000 acres of beets.

It is mostly
labour, is it not?
Labour is one problem.

It is the main
problem.

The
price is another factor. This year, on a sixteen per cent sugar content, these sugar beets would give the grower a gross return of approximately $100 per acre, and the average sugar content of the beets in those southern Ontario counties over the past ten years has been approximately sixteen per cent. But that return was not sufficient, particularly in view of labour difficulties and also having regard to other field crops, to bring about the maximum production of sugar beets in this country.
I do not know just what is the solution. It has been stated publicly that if we produced an additional 75,000,000 pounds of sugar we would have ample for our own use. That may be true, but, as the minister has said, if we brought about that additional production we would get approximately that much less from the United States. As the minister explained, our policy is coordinated1 with that of the United States in regard to sugar. Formerly we obtained the great bulk of our supplies under a trade treaty with the British West Indies. That has been cut off, owing to the lack of shipping space, and also to the fact that most

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
of the south Pacific islands are in Japanese hands, and now our sugar comes from Cuba, whose production is controlled by the government of the United States. So that now we buy our sugar through the United States, and if we produced an additional 75,000,000 pounds of our own we would probably get that much less from the United States. Our 75,000,000 pounds would simply go into the pool, to be divided among the people of Canada and the United States, and this would not make a great deal of difference to the average person who is doing some canning, or to the amount of sugar the average purchaser would get.
What I rose to say was that the sugar beet industry has been bandied around for a long time. The government of the day should make up its mind whether it wants sugar beets to grow in this country, or whether it does not. That is something the government does not seem to be able to do.

Last night the Minister of Finance promised that he would put on record certain figures respecting tire sales in the district of Mont Laurier. Would he be good enough to do that now, if the figures are not confidential? Then, is it true that the central office of the wartime prices and trade board in Montreal, Quebec or Ottawa establishes a quota on sales of tires in each territorial district? If so, how does that quota operate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot explain the operation of the quota very well, because it is established by the rubber controller rather than by the wartime prices and trade board. The rubber controller is an official of the Department of Munitions and Supply.
I would have to take out of the police report the figures for which the hon. member has asked. I do not think I should place on the record the figures showing the sales of half a dozen competing garages. I believe, however, that I might place on record the percentages, so as to bring out the point I made last night.
I said last night that the sales in 1942 by the Laurin garage were sharply up from the previous year, whereas the sales of the other five garages were sharply dowm. That is correct. The percentages I shall give are only approximate, and they may be slightly misleading because the fiscal years of the various garages are not the same. One would run from April to April, another from November to November; another would be the calendar year and so on. But approximately it would be true to say that sales of tires and tubes of the Laurin garage were double in 1942 what they were in 1941, or that they were 200 per cent of the 1941 figure. The 1942 sales of the
Gaston Forget garage were approximately twenty-five per cent of the 1941 sales. It is, however, fair to say that this percentage does not cover quite a twelve-month period. The 1942 sales of the William Grenier garage were approximately thirty per cent of the 1941 sales. The 1942 sales of the Grenier Brothers garage were approximately twenty-five per cent of the 1941 sales. The 1942 sales of the Vanchestein garage were approximately forty per cent of the 1941 sales. The 1942 sales of the Brisebois garage were approximately eighty-five per cent of the 1941 sales.
These figures had to be picked out of a confidential police report and converted into percentages. As I have said, allowances will have to be made for differences in the fiscal years, and in at least one case a period shorter than the fiscal year has been taken. That affects, of course, the validity of the comparison.

I thank the minister for this information. While we are on the subject of tires, I would point out that in my humble opinion the establishment of a quota for each district may lead to some misunderstanding. In fact, my information is that if a customer comes before the representative of the wartime prices and trade board with an application signed before a friendly garage, the quota is open to him. But if he comes with an application signed before a garage not friendly to the representative, then he is told, "Too bad, my friend; the quota is exhausted." I have received many complaints from my district regarding the handling of tire sales permits. The figures given by the minister this afternoon are an explanation of what has happened in my constituency. I am not surprised to see that the Laurin garage percentage has increased to the extent indicated, because Laurin and the representative of the board at Mont Laurier are very close friends. If the investigators of the wartime prices and trade board wish to make any further investigation, they would do well to see a certain number of persons in my district who would be only too glad to state that when they went to the representative's office with an application signed by a garage other than the Laurin garage they have always been told that this famous quota is exhausted.
I urge the minister to find a means of cutting down this practice which seems to be open to representatives of the calibre of the one at Mont Laurier. I thank the minister just the same for the trouble he has taken, and I would sincerely hope that in the near future he would keep a tight grip on the arrogant bureaucracy now prevailing in the district of Montreal, so far as the wartime prices and trade board is concerned.
