I have here a letter dated June 18, 1943, sent out by a large wholesale clothing company to all its branches. It is as follows:
There has been a ruling just put into force by the wartime prices and trade board saying that our khaki tropical worsted can be made in air force officers uniforms only. So if you get an army man or a navy man wanting a uniform of the wool tropical do not take the order, as we are not allowed to make them. The government is supplying the cloth, and they are reserving it for the air force only.
Why should the wartime prices and trade boardl discriminate against the army and the navy? Is it because the air force has such a pull that they can get that kind of goods, while the other armed forces cannot? These are materials for officers' uniforms. Surely there must be some explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is this from a wholesaler?

It is from a wholesale house to its branches. Officers of the army-I do not know about the navy- are pretty well upset about it and are wondering why a ruling like that should come out from the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall have to get information about that.

I mentioned the matter when the estimates of the Minister of Munitions and Supply were before us. It is something that should be cleared up at once, because there should be no necessity for these officers to go around in heavy uniforms if they can get the others. There should not be that type of discrimination. Officers of the air force are allowed to have bellows pockets in their uniforms, but the officers of the army or the navy are not allowed these. Uniforms fit better with this type of pocket, especially when an officer is carrying his order book or anything else in his pocket. I think the minister should look into the matter at once.
Last evening the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated that many employees of the wartime prices and trade board were receiving salaries of $4,000 or more. I do not object to their receiving salaries of that kind, although some of these men perhaps were not receiving any salaries in 1939. Many of them were attending university. I should like to cite the case of a sole proprietor who was doing a business of $30,000 or $40,000 a year in 1939 and taking out of the business only something like $2,500. Anything above that was being put back into the business. This man is not allowed to-day to take out

any more than the $2,500, even though he has increased his business, which may be an essential one, to $160,000 or $170,000 a year. I believe there is a point where he can take fifteen or twenty per cent, which would bring him up to $3,500 or $3,600. This man is making for the government $15,000 in excess profits tax and $4,000 or more in standard profits tax, but he is kept down to $3,500. He is not allowed1 to go up to the $5,000 salary limit, but men in the employ of the government, in the wartime prices.and trade board, have had their salaries jumped from $6,000 to $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not-
There is one man who had his salary raised from $6,600 to $10,000, and there are others who have had their salaries jumped up, although perhaps not that much.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be a promotion to a different job.

It might be a different job, but this sole proprietor of an essential business is doing a different job. In 1939 he may have been working only six hours a day, but to-day with the lack of help he is working eighteen hours a day; he is sales manager, treasurer, cashier and everything else. He is working for this government; he is working for you and for me, and he should be allowed to jump his salary to $5,000 the same as other government men have jumped theirs. If one man is allowed to do it, another man should be allowed to do it.
It is up to the government to see that these sole proprietors are not discriminated against. I know of two or three cases, but I have this one particularly in mind. I have not given the exact figures, but they are pretty close. This man has been held down to $3,600 and, as I said before, he is making for the government $15,000 in excess profits tax and $4,000 in standard profits tax. In 1940 about all the government got was the income tax on his $2,400 salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This scarcely comes under the resolution. For a while I thought the hon. gentleman was discussing salary control, but apparently he is discussing the administrative practices of the Department of National Revenue.
That is salary control.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not in the ordinary sense. Just let me make it clear. The sole proprietor is getting no salary' because he is employer

War Appropriation-
-Finance-
-Prices Board
and employee in the one person. The only importance of the point at all is for tax purposes-how much will the Department of National Revenue allow him to call salary for taxation purposes? It is not a question of salary for salary control purposes; it is merely a taxation problem, and it would not come under this resolution.
It comes under the wartime prices and trade board; they are the ones who regulate salaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They do not have anything to do with salaries; the salary controller does not have anything to do with this kind of thing. It is a matter of what the income tax branch will allow to be called salary for the purpose of computing the taxation of the company. That does not come under wartime prices and trade board; it is a matter for my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue.
Must your department go to the income tax commissioner when it jumps up a salary from $3,000 to $5,000 or $10,000, or do you just go ahead and do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not talking about the salary order; he is talking about the relationship between an employer and an employee. The salary in that case would be subject to the provisions of the salary control order. This matter is administered by the commissioner of income tax, who has a board to assist him. I do not want my hon. friend to get the idea that salaries are being jumped in the civil service. Where there are promotions, the appointees take the salaries of the higher positions. I may say that there has been a great deal of criticism, amounting almost to resentment, because of what is alleged to be harsh treatment accorded to the civil service. I would be glad to have my hon. friend's rebuttal on that.
I said that I did not object to the salaries being paid, but I said that they should all be equal. If you give it to one, you should give it to the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The same principles are applied.

Among other duties, I believe the wartime prices and trade board is charged with the responsibility of making decisions in connection with prices of foodstuffs. I think it was in February when the minister made a statement about the relationship between the wartime prices and trade board and the
Department of Agriculture, particularly the agricultural food board which has been set up by that department to deal with questions relating to foodstuffs, food production and distribution. It was apparent from the minister's statement that there has been a certain amount . of overlapping and uncertainty, and even open conflict, with regard to the jurisdiction of these boards. The minister stated that there had been a blurring of the lines of responsibility between the wartime prices and trade board and the Department of Agriculture and that there had been detailed consultations between the departments concerned. He stated also that as a result of conferences between the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and himself, a full understanding of the responsibilities of the two boards had been reached and overlapping had been eliminated. He then gave a detailed statement as to the authority of the two boards. He said that the wartime prices and trade board was charged with (1) responsibility of estimating and defining the over-all domestic needs for food; (2) responsibility for import and distribution of food; (3) final responsibility in all matters of price and final responsibility in all matters of consumer rationing.
The duties of the agricultural food board were defined as follows: (1) responsibility for maintaining and encouraging production; (2) consulting with the wartime prices and trade board as to subsidies and price adjustments; (3) recommendations to council re producer subsidies; (4) the exportation of foodstuffs, and (5) the diversion of foods to the armed forces.
In passing I should like to point out to the committee that these two boards, with a number of other agriculture boards, deal with farm problems; at least, they deal with farm prices. They influence farm income; in fact they practically control the whole economic set-up of agriculture to-day in Canada.
The finance minister stated in February that this division of authority was clear, but I am afraid that overlapping and misunderstanding are bound to continue. Several members of the different agricultural boards have just recently appeared before the committee on agriculture and colonization, where questions were constantly arising which had to do with the functions of the wartime prices and trade board and the relationship of price to production. The reluctance of the members of these agricultural boards to make any statement regarding the activities of the wartime prices and trade board was sufficient evidence, to my mind at least, that misunderstandings still exist and that there is not yet a clear division of authority.
4446	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
The most important factor to be considered in the encouragement, maintenance and increase of production, which is stated to be the first function of the food board, is necessarily that of price. If prices are not satisfactory, production cannot be maintained, let alone be increased. No one knows better than the Minister of Agriculture that this is so; for, speaking in the house on the demand for greater production of cheese some time ago, the minister instanced how the price of cheese in the winter months of 1941-42 had been raised to stimulate production, and he gave figures to show that when the price was raised, production increased substantially. If price is the main factor, how can the food board and other agricultural boards function properly to maintain and increase production, if price is controlled by another board over which they have no control, and which they can only consult.
I am firmly of the opinion that any control of the price of farm products should be vested in the boards which are responsible for the encouragement of production. The food board and other agricultural boards should be in the best position to deal with matters of price and production. Price and production go together; they cannot be managed by separate authorities. I believe that if price control of farm products had been vested in agricultural boards much dissatisfaction and uncertainty would have been avoided.
No one will deny that the price for farm products should be sufficiently high to cover the cost of efficient production and give a reasonable profit to the producer.
Nor can it be denied that in many lines of farm production the price ceiling as established by the wartime prices and trade board on the finished product has not been high enough to create a proper relationship between the price paid to the farmer for his goods, and that of the goods which he must buy. I have stated on more than one occasion that price control is necessary. We cannot allow inflation to run riot. But I am equally certain that price ceilings on farm products should not be imposed which do not establish parity as between the farmer's prices and those of other products. I therefore reaffirm my belief that one of two courses should have been followed by the wartime prices and trade board. The first one would be that until prices of farm products have risen to the point where there is parity, no price ceiling should be established on foodstuffs which come from the Canadian farm; or, second, ceilings providing parity should have been set up in1 the first instance. It is true
fMr. Senn.]
that the Minister of Agriculture early in the session gave certain figures, which appear in Hansard, endeavouring to show that parity exists already. His definition of parity, however, is theoretical and academic. It reads as follows:
Parity price is the price of the commodity which will give a purchasing power with respect to articles the farmer buys equivalent to the purchasing power of such commodity in the base period.
If we assume for a moment that this is a correct definition, it will be readily seen that a base period during which parity existed should be chosen for purposes of comparison. Certainly farmers will not agree that parity existed at the time chosen by the minister, namely, the period between 1926 and 1929. As a matter of fact, the inequalities in prices which existed at that time, and for years before, was one of the chief causes leading to the depression which began in 1929. The fact remains, however, as the minister knows, and certainly as producers know, that farm prices were entirely out of line in the period chosen, September 15 to October 12, 1941, which served as a basis of present ceilings above which prices of foodstuffs are prohibited from going. It is the season when large quantities of farm products are being marketed and when prices are generally lower than the yearly average. Seasonal conditions are largely responsible for these low prices. It is the period when grain has been threshed, when farmer's commitments become due and when taxes must be paid. He must sell to raise money to meet these demands, and he is convinced that his necessity is often exploited by the concerns that process and market his goods.
I feel certain that the price received from exportable surpluses of farm products would in large measure prevent excessive rises in price, because the domestic price is largely governed by the price received for such exportable surpluses. If shortages arise which might tend to boost prices above a reasonable level, rationing as it is being practised by the wartime prices and trade board would finally effectively control such rises.
The question will then be asked if, when prices of farm products rise to a position of parity in Canada, will that increase the cost of living and create dissatisfaction among the consumers in the urban centres? I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that in such cases, instead of providing producer subsidies, which are more or less hand-outs to the Canadian farmer, consumer subsidies should be given, if necessary, to protect the interests of the consumer. We have at the present time one specific

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
example of consumer subsidies which is working satisfactorily. The farmer is fairly well satisfied with the price he receives for milk destined for fluid consumption. The consumer is protected by a consumer subsidy on milk of two cents a quart, which keeps the price to the consumer at a reasonable level. In my judgment the same method should be applied by these boards to other commodities if we are to encourage production, and if price is to be the deciding factor in so doing.
I do not want to carry on to any great extent, but I should like to say that the same conditions that have applied between the bacon and meat board and the wartime prices and trade board exist also with the dairy industry. Milk is processed into a number of products, all of which are important as food. But on these products arbitrary price ceilings have been imposed, just the same as in other lines of foodstuffs. In the case of dairy products, as in the case of bacon, the price realized for the processed article influences in great measure the amount of production in the different lines of dairy products. Instead of prices of dairy products being allowed to find their own level and thus stimulate and encourage production, a rigid control, often unevenly applied, has been practised. I am not objecting to control, but the unevenness of the control is a matter which, I think, should be criticized, and it has resulted in confusion, rivalry and distrust in the dairy industry. It is comparatively easy for milk producers to change the factory to which they send their milk; in fact, they can change overnight from a cheese factory to a butter factory, or to a condensary. Some discussion was had a short time ago respecting the power of the dairy products board or of the food board to determine the destination of the farmers' milk. To exercise such power, even in a roundabout way or by moral suasion, is, in my judgment, interfering too much with personal liberty.
The whole point of the argument which I have been attempting to make is that price ceilings on food should not have been established at levels lower than are commensurate with the cost of production and at levels lower than those set for other commodities which the farmer has to buy. Great care should be taken to study carefully every implication and every possible result of price fixing and control before making an order. Too often after an order is made, same unforeseen complication follows which, in turn, has to be remedied until the whole system is a patchwork puzzle which confuses and discourages the producer.
Agriculture in Canada is fully aware of the vital need of food production as part of our war effort. It has made almost superhuman
efforts to produce to capacity. In this it has been blessed by Providence with favourable weather conditions resulting in bumper crops. It has been, however, and is still handicapped by labour shortages and insufficient cash returns.
I once more urge upon the minister and his colleagues the advisability of placing the price structure of food products where it properly belongs, namely under the control of the Minister of Agriculture and the agricultural boards.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I should say at once that I believe that would be a great mistake. It is essential in every price control system that the control of all prices be vested in one body, one authority. If the setting of prices on agricultural products were to be removed from the authority of the wartime prices and trade board and transferred to the Department of Agriculture, there would be an equally good reason for removing control of fishery products from the wartime prices and trade board and placing it in the Department of Fisheries, and, as a matter of fact, for removing the prices of products of the mines and the forests and placing it under the jurisdiction of the Department of Mines and Resources. In fact, the only theory on which there should be that spreading around of authority is that it is desirable to put the control of prices in the hands of persons who are directly concerned with production and who traditionally have concerned themselves more intimately with the interests of producers.
That is a very popular theory, and it does not apply only to farmers; it applies to a great many groups in this country who would like to get their prices away from the wartime prices and trade board. I repeat, they would just love to get their prices away from the wartime prices and trade board, because they would hope to be in a little more sympathetic forum when they applied for higher prices. That would be their reason. I am not saying that against them. I am not saying that against the hon. gentleman who is advocating it. He speaks in this house for the farmers and argues the farmers' case on a good many occasions, and that is his right. But the reason I have given is the reason why these groups want to get somewhere else; they would like to get some place where, they think, they would be dealing with individuals who would be less concerned with control and more concerned with higher prices.
We have to take hold of this thing or drop it. We have to be firm, or we have to be vacillating.
I am utterly convinced of the unsoundness of the suggestion made by the hon. member

4448	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
for Haldimand when he says that we should carve out one set of prices and take that away from the price control authority; because you cannot separate one set of prices from other prices. A great many farm products are used in the production of processed products. Would the price of the processed product be left under the jurisdiction of the wartime prices and trade board when the price of the primary product was placed'under the jurisdiction of some other authority? Would the price of competing imports be left under the jurisdiction of the wartime prices and trade board and the price of primary products in Canada be transferred to some other authority? As a matter of fact, if the pace of price control were to be set by various competing authorities, with a central price control authority, the administrative task of * the central price control authority would be impossible and they might as well go out of business. That is the reason why I have always urged and argued that there be one price control authority for all prices. I am sure that no other system of price control would work.
With reference to the other point which the hon. gentleman has argued, with regard to parity prices and prices on farm products,
I think, if we talked about that, we would talk endlessly. It has been discussed and discussed and discussed in this chamber every time the Minister of Agriculture comes before the house, and I have made some speeches on it from time to time over the last two or three years. It has been repeatedly emphasized by public men in other countries as well as by public men in this country that if you intend to institute price control you have to start some time, you cannot go on partly adjusting before you start. We thought the time had come in the fall of 1941 when we had to start, and, as I said the other day, I am convinced we did the right thing and did it at the right time. We made some adjustments afterwards. We made most of our adjustments by way of subsidies, and the subsidy bill is very substantial indeed. As a matter of fact, the difference between producers' subsidies and consumers' subsidies is not as great as hon. gentlemen seem to think; it is a difference in form rather than in principle. When we pay a subsidy of ten cents a pound on butter we are doing so for the benefit of the consumer, are we not; as much as for the benefit of the producer? The consumer is enabled by the payment of that subsidy to get his butter for thirty-five cents a pound, and the producer is enabled by the payment of that subsidy to get forty-five cents a pound for it. I do not see that 
there is very much difference in principle, although there is a difference in form, between that and the milk subsidy, which has the effect of enabling the producer to get whatever the price is-say, twelve cents-and the consumer nevertheless to get milk for ten cents a quart.

The hon. member for Mackenzie a little while ago suggested that the minister might regard himself somewhat as the father of his country. If he does so regard himself, I believe we should bring to his attention one matter which is of great importance in a country like -ours. I have had representations from small retail stores selling children's clothing and children's underwear, and also letters from young mothers-to-be on the extreme shortage of yard goods which are needed for babies' layettes and young babies' clothing. I think the minister is familiar with that square garment which constitutes the major portion of a baby's wardrobe in its early years. Really there is an appalling shortage of cotton goods, mostly flannelette. I had word from one store in Vancouver that they were able to sell only five yards of flannelette to every layette. That is positively absurd, and there are hundreds, indeed thousands of young mothers-to-be who are frantic, because they do not know where to get the material they need. The question of price is also important. Twenty-five or thirty-five cents a yard used to be considered a reasonable price for a good quality of flannelette, and at that price it was decent enough for most mothers; but now the price is roughly fifty cents, which makes the cost of the layette for the working mother considerably greater. Even in the white *wool for small coaties for very young babies there is an extreme shortage. This is a matter of importance to thousands of young people, and I suggest that the minister might look into this shortage, particularly of yard goods and flannelette, and see to it that an adequate amount is allowed. I am informed by one retail store in Vancouver that 230,000

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
yards of flannelette is being released this year, but that is totally inadequate to provide for the number of layettes expected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been an increasing demand for flannelette, and the board is fully conscious of the present situation and has taken steps to limit the use of flannelette for certain purposes and to order the production of greater quantities. It is a problem with which the board is quite familiar and on which it is working.
What about the price? Does that necessarily have to be greater, or will they keep the price down? At present it is fifty cents and that is exorbitant.

speechtext:
May I refer to a question raised by the hon. member for Haldimand. There are one or two questions I would ask with respect to it. AVhat is the basis of determining the subsidies paid on various agricultural products? Observing these subsidies, it has been difficult for me to find out any basis on which they are paid. It seems to me that the basis has been simply that when a certain product became scarce the department gave a subsidy to secure greater production, and there
does not appear to be any basis, or equal basis, for different products, on which the subsidy is calculated. If that is the principle on which the subsidies are paid, then the only way in which agriculture can get a fair price for its products is to have a shortage, and when the shortage becomes apparent the subsidy is immediately paid. That appears to be a poor method by which to get extra production. We are going to be scarce of a good many agricultural products this year. From evidence we have had before the committee on agriculture it is doubtful whether we shall be able to supply the amount required by the British government this year in any agricultural product with the exception of wheat. Certainly in dried potatoes, vegetables, dried eggs and cheese, the situation is doubtful. I d'oubt whether we shall obtain the production that they require without further seriously curtailing the amount for home consumption in Canada. Price is a determining factor in the amount of agricultural commodities produced. Take eggs. Last winter they dropped nineteen cents a dozen in the month of January, and immediately there was a serious curtailment in the production. While these conditions prevail, unless agriculture is guaranteed a market in which the farmers know they will get a certain price for their products, the production required will not be obtained.
As regards transferring authority for the payment of these subsidies from the wartime prices and trade board to the Department of Agriculture, I certainly think agriculture would get more favourable treatment from the Department of Agriculture than from the board. That does not necessarily mean that the price ceiling would be pierced. You can pierce the ceiling in two different ways, by making articles scarce and by creating a black market, or by the other method. The policy being followed by the wartime prices board is one that is creating a scarcity of agricultural products, and I suggest, therefore, that the basis on which the subsidies are paid should be the cost of production. I have argued this point with the minister before, and he says it is impossible to ascertain the cost of production of agricultural products because every farm is different. They find the cost of production of war goods and pay different prices to different factories on the same goods. I maintain that the cost of production of agricultural products can be ascertained, not necessarily on every farm, but a fair base price could be ascertained and the subsidies could be paid on that basis instead of by the haphazard method by which they are now paid.

The minister stated that the Department of Agriculture made recommendations to the wartime prices and trade

board with respect to subsidies. Are these recommendations accepted? That is the point in which I am interested.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not quite correct. The precise position is that the Minister of Agriculture consults with the wartime prices and trade board and then makes such recommendations to council as he thinks fit with respect to subsidies to primary producers. Whether or not council accepts his recommendations depends, of course, upon the view they take of the matter at the time. They have to give consideration to all the factors involved.
Then are we to take it for granted that the Department of Agriculture is responsible for prices?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; prices are wholly under the control of the wartime prices and trade board; that is, the prices that may be charged for the goods in the market; but the payment of subsidies, which is separate from prices, is a matter for council, and the recommendation to council comes from the Minister of Agriculture after the matter has been discussed with the price-fixing authority by the officials of the Department of Agriculture.
Has the wartime prices and trade board anything to do with the regulations of the prices of articles made from magnesium, zinc, rubber, beryllium, titanium, plastics and so forth?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; it has everything to do with the prices if they are civilian goods.
But not military goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The price ceiling does not apply to purchases by the Department of Munitions and Supply. They have the right by law to pay more than the maximum price and have done so on occasion when they found it necessary in order to get what they had to get. But more and more they are complying with the ceilings and working very closely with the wartime prices and trade board, giving the board every opportunity to get them the goods at or below the ceiling.

I know it is important to get the munitions, but on the other hand a great deal of important material came out before the United States senate committee dealing with patents and so on which indicated that prices were being enhanced through the control of patents, the restriction of production and the control of materials through cartels and so forth. As a result, the assistant attorney general of the United States, Thurman

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
W. Arnold, appeared before that committee and asked for specific legislation to prevent the United States from being compelled to pay enhanced prices through restrictions on patents and so on. On July 31, 1942, he asked that legislation be passed to prevent-
. . . the use of patents as an instrument to suppress competition, restrict production or destroy independent business on a scale that substantially interferes with the distribution of any commodity.
And which results in the enhancing of prices. I have been wondering what we have in this country. We do not have a committee set up to go into these matters, as they have in the United States Senate, nor I suppose, have we officials such as they have in that country to control these prices, unless the wartime prices and trade board exercises such control. The minister says it does not have that control in relation to goods supplied for military purposes. It is well known that aviation gasoline, rubber, beryllium, titanium, magnesium, zinc and so on are all under the control of patents and cartels, most of them international in scope. Is Canada being protected now, as the United States is, against the payment of enhanced prices for such articles even if they are required for military purposes? I agree that the main purpose is to get the materials; that is all-important; but on the other hand there should be some control in regard to prices, even where materials are purchased- for war purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only repeat what I said, that whether they are cartelized or not, no matter how they are handled or by whom, when they are sold to a civilian purchaser they must comply with the price ceiling. It is well known that this price ceiling runs through hundreds of thousands of different articles, and that they cannot go beyond it. That does not apply, as I said before, to sales made to the Department of Munitions and Supply. As a matter of practice, I think they do buy at or below ceiling prices in nearly all cases. They have their controllers, their buyers, their organizations; they do not pay any more than they have to, but for the reasons I gave the other night and again to-day they are exempted by law from the operation of the ceilings.

In connection with
magnesium metal they are paying a very much higher price than that given to the house a year ago by the Minister of Munitions and Supply as the price at which magnesium metal would likely be made in this country. Who controls the selling price of magnesium metal made for the Department of Munitions and Supply? Do the producers set any prices they wish? I am quoting from memory and
I may be wrong, but I believe the price I mentioned in this house recently was forty cents a pound, or a cent or two one way or the other. That is a very high price for magnesium metal, which was offered to the government by another company at a very much lower price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The price is set by the Department of Munitions and Supply, for reasons which appear good to them.
Then there is no control over what is paid by the Department of Munitions and Supply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not under this legislation. It is controlled by order in council; that is, the contracts are approved by order in council.

For the expert statistician this is perhaps sufficient, but I feel that the committee would appreciate some general comments of a less technical nature which may help to explain just how the index is prepared and what it means. These are based in the main on information supplied by the bureau of statistics.
The index is a measure of the month to month changes in the cost of living of the average Canadian wage-earner's family. In 1937 and 1938 the bureau made a study of the living expenses of nearly 1,500 Canadian families. These families were specially picked as typical wage-earning families; each consisted of a husband and wife and one child or more. The average number of people in the family was 4-6, and the average family income was $1,453 a year. Officials from the bureau asked these families to keep a careful record of their expenditures during the twelve months from October, 1937, to September, 1938. It was on the basis of these records that the bureau knew how much importance to give to the various kinds of food, clothing, recreation and all other things that come into the family budget. They divided the cost of living up into the six main groups and found that they occupied the following proportions of the average living expenses of the families that were surveyed: food 31 per cent, fuel and light 6 per cent, housing 19 per cent, clothing 12 per cent, home furnishings and services 9 per cent, miscellaneous items 23 per cent.
It has been argued that conditions have changed a good deal since that budget was prepared in 1937 and 1938. There are some goods that cannot be bought to-day, and the purchase of other goods is limited by rationing. I want to make it clear that the bureau takes such changes as these into account. For example, automobile tires and tubes, steel frying pans, and bananas have been removed from the index since they are no longer regularly available. The weighting given to tea, sugar and motor operating costs has been reduced on account of rationing. Some changes in buying habits are so small as to have a negligible effect on the index, and in such cases, of course, there is no point in making adjustment. I should also point out that when the bureau takes an item from the index, that does not mean that the total living expenditures have been reduced. The amount of money that was formerly spent on these articles is regarded as being distributed among other items in the index.
It is important to realize that the index aims to record a fixed standard of living. During the war, and particularly during its early
years, many families increased their family income, and- as a result have bought better clothes, more expensive food, etcetera. The index does not and should not record higher living expenses due to better living. If it did it would indicate not a higher cost of living but a higher standard of living.
Now, let me revert for a moment to one of the most frequently expressed criticisms of the index. Many people want to know how it can possibly be maintained that the cost of living has only gone up 17 per cent during the war in view of the rise which has taken place in foods. They point to stewing beef which has risen by 78 per cent, lard which has risen by 73 per cent, round steak which has risen by 66 per cent during the war, and so on.
It is perfectly true that those particular foods have risen by that amount, but the committee should remember that they represent only a small part of the cost of living. All foods put together represent less than a third of the cost of living index, and while some foods have risen substantially, other foods such as bread, sugar, etcetera, have remained steady, and milk has actually declined in price. These are important foods, and occupy a much larger part in the weekly family budget than many of those foods which have risen in price.
Foods in the cost of living index have risen by 31-8 per cent since the beginning of the war. This is a substantial rise, most of which occurred before the application of the price ceiling. It is also the part of the cost of living of which the housewife is particularly aware since she sees the effect of it upon her allowance for housekeeping expenses. The other items, which in many households are paid by the husband, have not risen by anything like this amount since the beginning of the war. Fuel and light have risen by 14-1 per cent, housing by 7-4 per cent, clothing by 20-3 per cent, home furnishings and services by 16-7 per cent, and miscellaneous items by 6-8 per cent. The total index has risen by 17-6 per cent since August, 1939, but of this only 2-2 per cent since the establishment of the ceiling.
The point I want to make here is that the cost of food has risen by more than the other groups in the index, and the cost of certain particular food items has risen by a good deal more than the cost of food as a whole. Now many people tend to regard the cost of living as just the cost of food. They forget that the cost of living also includes rent, and clothing, and electric light, and life insurance, and doctors' bills, and many other needs which have increased in price a great deal less than has food.

Another question which is frequently asked concerns the accuracy of the price reports made to the bureau.
The bureau does not rely entirely on reports from storekeepers. In addition to the reports which it receives from storekeepers, it has its own representative in most of the principal regional centres, and it may appoint others before long. These representatives obtain the prices needed each month by personal visits to stores. It may interest the committee to know that these representatives periodically visit smaller towns so as to make a check on the trend of prices throughout the region.
I should now like to say a word on deterioration of quality, which is a live topic at the moment. For many years the bureau has asked firms reporting prices for clothing and home furnishings to make at the same time estimates of any changes of quality in the goods. When the bureau receives a report of a reduction in quality, this reduction is treated just as if it were a price increase of the same amount. The bureau, furthermore, instructs its field representatives to 'be on the watch for quality deterioration when obtaining price reports.
It must be remembered that there are two types of quality deterioration:	that which
shortens the life of an article, and that which affects its appearance without shortening its life or reducing its serviceability. If a man finds that a suit now stands only three quarters of the wear that a similar suit used to stand, the cost of his clothes over a period of years has risen, although the price remains the same. It is obviously reasonable to include deterioration of that type in the cost-of-living index. Suppose, on the other hand, the man finds that the suit he now buys is less attractive than it used to be, the material rougher perhaps or with less novelty in pattern but it still lasts every bit as long as it used to. He could not then claim that this quality deterioration had affected his cost of living.
There have been complaints that many cheap lines of goods are now off the market, and that it is necessary to buy more expensive brands. In such cases the bureau puts the price of the more expensive brands into the index. Stores have instructions not to report the price of any article winch is not readily available, but instead to send in the price of the next more expensive article that is readily available.
A list of the items included in the index has been published, and comments have been made on the large number of items entering into an average family's normal budget which are not on this list. These omissions may be difficult to understand but the reason is that 
it is not practicable to get direct price quotations for every item in the family budget. The bureau instead obtains price reports on what are regarded as typical items, "weighting" those prices sufficiently highly to cover all the items that ought to be in the group. I would take as an instance, foods. Many foods have wide seasonal price changes, and as a result the consumption of them varies. People eat them in quantity when the price is low and eat less when the price is high. Shifts in consumption from season to season and year to year, as crops vary, are so great that it is extremely difficult to give these foods a correct degree of importance in the budget. There is also the problem of obtaining comparable prices.
* Many of the fresh vegetables in particular are not always sold upon a weight basis, so that price changes may actually reflect quantity differences as well. To include these items might well result in the index becoming less rather than more accurate.
The bureau of statistics, therefore, picks out those foods items on which a representative price can be obtained from month to month. . The index includes forty-four food items which represent about seventy-five per cent of the total cost of foods in the budget on which the index is based. Those foods on which a price is not obtained are considered to have risen by the same proportion as those foods on which price reports are made.
The bureau has often been asked whether the restricted number of foods in the index makes it less reliable. In order to test this possibility a check was made. An experimental food index was computed on the basis of only fifteen items; round steak, blade roast, rolled rib roast, pork loins, bacon, milk, butter, eggs, flour, sugar, potatoes, corn syrup, marmalade, oranges and lard. This index, with one-third of the items in the official index, shows a wartime rise to May, 1943, of 30-3 per cent, which is only 0-5 per cent less than the increase for foods shown in the official index. I might mention, incidentally, that the number of food items included in the Canadian index compares favourably with those in the indexes of other countries.
Food, of course, is not. the only group where difficulty is experienced in getting representative prices. Another difficult group is clothing, which also includes many items seasonal in character. A lady's hat may sell in season at S4.95 and be cleared at $2.98 or less. The same is true of dresses, coats, and many other items. To include prices for these things in the index would cause erratic movements which would not follow the basic changes in clothing prices. Therefore, the

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
bureau has selected a comparatively small list of twenty-nine clothing items which are of fairly standard construction and have no pronounced seasonal price movements. These items represent in proper proportion all the important materials used in making clothing, i.e., cotton, wool, rayon, rubber and leather. The bureau assumes and I think with reason, that the change in cost of these items gives a correct record of the rise or fall in all clothing prices.
Having dealt with the cost-of-living index itself I now wish to make a few remarks on related topics which are more strictly the concern of the Minister of Finance.
In the course of his remarks the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to the effect of direct taxes, such as income taxes, on the cost-of-living index. This is a question that is raised from time to time and I think merits a fairly full explanation. The hon. member said and I quote:
But the bureau apparently does not take into consideration any of the direct taxes paid toy the people of Canada. Yet these taxes have increased tremendously, and add to the cost of living.
If the committee will consider the matter carefully I think they will agree that to include direct taxes in the cost-of-living index would be quite inappropriate and would indeed defeat the whole purpose of our wartime financial programme.
The cost-of-living index measures changes in the cost of living of the average wage-earner's family. It is an index of prices like an index of wholesale prices or an index of retail prices. If prices go up the index goes up; if prices go down the index goes down. To the extent that taxes such as excise and customs taxes which are indirect taxes enter into prices, they are, of course, reflected in the index. The only exception to this is the increased war taxes on cigarettes and tobacco which were excluded for a specific and, I think, obvious reason.
Direct taxes, on the other hand, do not affect prices. They are taxes on incomes, that is, they reduce the amount available for spending. If the hon. member's argument were sound that direct taxes affect the cost of living, it would follow that the cost of living of the rich man had risen many times more rapidly than that of the man wfith a low or moderate income. Equally absurd, it would mean that the cost of living of the man with a family had risen less sharply than the cost of living of a single man with the same income.
I would also point out that if an attempt were made to include income taxes in the cost-of-living index, there would have to be an individual cost-of-living index for each taxpayer as taxes vary enormously from individual to individual depending upon income, family responsibilities and personal circumstances. An average would mean absolutely nothing.
But there is a very much more important reason for not including direct taxes in the cost-of-living index. When, as acting Minister of Finance, I delivered the first Canadian war budget speech on September 12, 1939, I said:
We shall be guided by the belief that all our citizens will be ready to bear some share of the cost of the war, but we shall insist on the principle of equality of sacrifice on the basis of ability to pay.
If income taxes were included in the index, this principle would be nullified, for since the cost-of-living bonus is determined by the cost-of-living index the bonus would be increased by approximately the amount of the increase in the income tax. Thus people getting the bonus would1 pay little or no income tax. Furthermore, it is to be remembered that only certain groups are eligible for the bonus. To these, in effect, taxes paid would be rebated, leaving more to be borne by those who are not eligible for the bonus.
The hon. member then went on to say, and I want to deal particularly with this phase of his argument, that "part of the money paid in taxes is being used to subsidize prices. Part of what we pay in taxes is actually part of the price which we pay for some of our food." The hon. member appears to be arguing that the policy of paying subsidies in order to stabilize the cost of living is a case of transferring money from one pocket into the other, of robbing Peter to pay Paul.
The truth is, of course, that subsidies designed to keep down' the cost of living serve a very definite and useful purpose and that, used judiciously, they are essential to any general policy of price stabilization, serving the dual purpose of ensuring supply and of protecting the standards of life and of those receiving low or moderate incomes.
A rise in the cost of living produces unequal effects upon various sections of the population. It is true that some individuals might manage to cover the added costs of living by the increases in their incomes resulting from higher prices. Perhaps the unmarried industrial worker drawing cost-of-living bonus would be in that fortunate position. But his fellow worker, married and with a family, is not so well placed. His cosbofi-

As to the cost of subsidies, this is borne, not ini proportion to benefits received-then it would be a meaningless transfer from one pocket to the other-but like any other war cost, in accordance with ability to pay. The family man who benefits most firom stabilized living costs pays his share of subsidy costs not directly in proportion to the benefits received but, on the contrary, according to his taxes, which vary inversely in proportion to the number of his dependents. Rich and poor benefit in proportion to what they consume; they pay in accordance with their income. In- other words, the payment of subsidies distributes the burden of rising costs according to ability to pay. Far from being a policy of robbing Peter to pay Paul, the payment of subsidies to stabilize the cost of living is sound and in the best interests of the very groups in the community on whose behalf my hon. friend so often speaks.

The matter of enforcement was referred to last evening by the hon. member for Lake Centre. The minister also had something to say on that this afternoon, although I think I did not quite follow him. My understanding is that in the first place a recommendation is made by the local investigator that a .prosecution be instituted, that the local office sends it on to the provincial counsel, who is a permanent official retained by the government to look after these matters, and that provincial counsel then sends the whole file on to Ottawa, where the matter is dealt with by the enforcement administrator here, who I understand, is Mr. F. A. McGregor. I asked a question in the house on the enforcement division last March. My question was:
What are the names of the administrators and other officials of the enforcement division of the wartime prices and trade -board situated in the city of Ottawa?

I was informed in reply that Mr. F. A. McGregor was the enforcement administrator, that he was a permanent official of the Department of Labour at Ottawa, and that there were two other -members of the division, Mr. H. M. Brown, deputy enforcement administrator, also a permanent official of the Department of Labour, Ottawa, and Mr. P. J. M. MacDonald, enforcement counsel. My understanding is that one of these three gentlemen is a barrister by profession. It is this board of three which in the final analysis determines whether or not a prosecution shall be instituted.
Under the provisions of the order in council under which the prosecutions are instituted, it is necessary to obtain consent in writing from the wartime prices and trade board or from the attorney general of -the province concerned before an information can be laid. The prosecution is a very technical one, and I suggest to the minister that this whole matter should be left in the hands of some competent counsel who has experience in prosecutions and that it should not be left in the hands of this board of three sitting in Ottawa. I say that for a particular reason. I have personal knowledge of one case in which Mr. McGregor insisted on a prosecution despite the fact that he had been advised by the local counsel in Saskatchewan that -the consents necessary before the information was laid were not proper consents, and that a conviction could not be obtained. As a matter of fact, because these consents were not proper, seventeen charges were dismissed. I suggest to the minister that since these prosecutions are very technical, as he knows as well as I, if not better, they should be in charge of some man who is well trained in such matters. I am not for one minute suggesting that they have not trained men in the provinces; I know they have in Saskatchewan, but my point is that prosecutions should be in the hands of someone who has a greater knowledge of prosecutions than this board of individuals who reside in the city of Ottawa.

The point I was going to make is this. I understand that the quality of gasoline which is sold now is not as high as that sold during the price-ceiling period. I understand that this matter was taken up with the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, because the complaint was that a gallon of gasoline is now of inferior quality, probably for reasons which are beyond the control of the administration; I do not know. But if that is the fact, I should like to know why steps have not been taken to review the cost of gasoline to the consumer, because if with a gallon of gasoline you could go, say twenty-five miles in 1941, and with a gallon of gasoline you can now go only fifteen miles, surely, if the price-ceiling policy is to be retained, some reduction in price should be made.
The other point to which I wish to refer seems to me to be of the utmost importance, and I should like to obtain some information from the minister in connection with it. I refer to the setting of a price. As the years have gone by since this price-ceiling policy was introduced, we have found that it is necessary to depart from it to a certain extent with respect to certain commodities. I have in mind particularly meat. At one time meats came under the original price-ceiling policy of the government, they had to be sold at the same price at which meats of a comparable quality were sold during the basic period. But since that time the whole set-up has been greatly changed, so that now we have prices set for lamb, pork, veal and so on by special orders in council. I wish to know from the minister the method by which it is determined that there should be a change in the price ceiling with respect to, say meat
or eggs, because I can see that the whole situation is fraught with a great deal of danger, particularly if the matter is not kept completely secret. I should like to know whether the decision is restricted to a very few people, or whether a number of people are called into consultation, and, generally speaking, just how the administration safeguards the public against the possibility of a change in the price ceiling leaking out before it is made effective.
I know very well that it is difficult to conceal these things. I must confess that I have been somewhat amazed, and have expressed this feeling before, that things which are supposed to be kept in the dark nevertheless seem to get out. For example, a short time before the minister brought down his budget a year ago he announced that the administration did not believe a policy of compulsory savings to be feasible, and yet two days before the minister made his speech in this house last year there was a little write-up in one of the local papers indicating that in all probability a system of compulsory savings would be brought in. I give that to the minister as an indication of the manner in which things may leak out, and I am very much afraid, in connection with the price-ceiling policy, that unless the most rigid control is kept over the matter of the deliberations of the people who have charge of these matters, there is great scope for possible dishonesty. I should like the minister to clear that up, for this reason. In the last few months there have been several changes in connection with the price ceiling on meat and also on eggs, and1 I have received inquiries from citizens in my own constituency with respect to the manner in which this was done. They have said to me-and I repeat this to the minister -"It is a strange thing that just before there is a rise in the price ceiling of meat, certain people are very active in the meat buying market." They say, "Either they have inside information"-which I am not necessarily suggesting-"or else they are pretty good guessers." I have known in my own city of meat buyers going to the stock yards and buying meat in tremendous quantities just before there happened to be a rise in the price ceiling. The same thing has happened with regard to eggs. I suggest that, in view of the feeling on the part of these people which I have mentioned, the minister should make a statement clearing up this situation.
I give the minister another example of what happened recently, in connection with* the matter of eggs. There was a change in the price, I have forgotten whether it was up or down, and in order to ensure that holders of

speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will look at the report of the wartime prices and trade board, he will find that at page 66 it is provided that the names of persons furnishing information to the board on enforcement matters are held confidential in the investigations which follow.

In connection with
administration costs which amount to $14,300,000, how are the personnel selected? How are those who are to be placed in charge of the various regional offices of the board selected, and what salaries do they receive? This question has to do with the ability of the staff to keep the public informed and to give the public accurate information. There is a multitude of orders in council being passed in regard to prices, and I should like to know what machinery exists in order to keep these officials informed, and what are their instructions with respect to giving information to the public. A person goes to the wartime prices office and asks for some information in regard to what rent should be charged for a room, or what he should do with some surplus coupons, or some other related matter in connection with which they require information. The complaint I have received is that these persons often are told to go and see a lawyer about it', that those in charge of these offices did not know what should be done, and admit it. I should like to know whether those employed in these offices are instructed to do this, or whether there is not some higher official in Ottawa from whom they can get the information they require.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is an important system of internal circularization; that is to say, the board orders, instructions and so on are sent round to the staff of the board in all parts of Canada. They are informed promptly as to everything it is necessary for them to know. It might be that some official would not take

it upon himself to advise an applicant on some legal question; that sometimes happens, and in a case like that it is better to tell the applicant to see a lawyer than to give bad legal advice.
Generally speaking, appointments to positions carrying salaries of under $5,000 are made by the civil service commission, and to those carrying salaries of over $5,000 by the governor in council. On the question of salaries it might be of interest for me to inform the committee that as of March 31, 1943, those serving without remuneration numbered 259; those receiving over $8,500 per annum, none; those receiving from $5,000 to $8,500, 43; those receiving from $4,001 to $5,000, 83; those receiving $3,001 to $4,000, 174; those receiving from $2,001 to $3,000, 683; and those receiving $2,000 and under, 3,723; making a total of 4,965 at that time. The average salary including cost of living bonus, based on salaries paid during the month of March, 1043, and including those serving without remuneration, was $1,525, while excluding all persons serving without remuneration the average annual salary, on the basis I have just given, was $1,610. Was that the information the hon. gentleman wanted about salaries?

Yes. The other question whether there is any source to which those in charge of these offices can refer in case they are asked something they cannot answer. Are they instructed to tell people making such inquiries to go and see a lawyer? Is there a source within the department to which they can refer such inquiries? *

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; they would go to their superiors for information. If their superiors did not have the information, they would apply to their superiors and finally it w'ould be obtained. You know sometimes people ask you the most annoying questions, and I can well understand that an official might hesitate to give an opinion which, unappreciated by the questioner, might have to do with a difficult point of law about which a lawyer should be consulted.

You send the annoying
question to a lawyer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I never like to be asked for a definite opinion on a difficult point of law, because it is a most dangerous question to answer.

In a wartime prices and trade board press release, dated July 6, I find the following:
Appointment of Irving B. Everett of Toronto to an executive position in the wartime prices and trade board's ration administration was

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
announced to-day. Mr. Everett will be chief of the general section in charge of meat and butter. Mr. Everett is on loan from the Swift Canadian Company, Limited, Toronto, of which he has been sales manager.
I am just wondering how many members of that board have been employed by these packing houses. In my own riding there is a man who has been slaughtering hogs for the last thirty or forty years; in fact I think he had the first private slaughtering place in our district. Now he has been denied a permit to slaughter hogs. He asked permission to slaughter just what one might call the runts in the different pens, and even that was refused him, though they said he would be allowed to slaughter farmers' hogs. It looks to me as though there is some discrimination against the small man who is slaughtering his own animals, or is slaughtering for others. I find this in the Globe and Mail of July 6:
The Central British Columbia Live Stock Association has sent an appeal to the dominion government asking that merchants holding slaughter permits be allowed to issue temporary permits to producers to slaughter live stock for sale to the merchants.
At another point they say:
The wartime prices and trade board recently decreed that slaughtering of live stock for local use in rural areas must be done .and stamped by one man. In the Burns-Francois lakes district, the man appointed by the local ration board was the only one who might be said to have an "abattoir"-two poplar trees growing beside a road.
The farmers complain that to obey the order they must in some cases hire trucks or hitch up the old grey mare and cart live stock anywhere from ten to one hundred miles to be butchered at the poplar tree abattoir.
I note that it is creating a hardship throughout the rural district, because these people who are forty or fifty miles, or perhaps more, away from packing houses cannot haul their hogs to those packing houses and then back home again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Everett, to whom the
hon. member referred, is chief of the rationing administration. The rationing administration has no connection with the food administration. It is in the food administration that the slaughtering control rests.

It
would be all mixed up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; they are distinctly
separate. The rationing administration is at Montreal, and the foods administration is at Ottawa. They are certainly distinct. It is [DOT]easy to say that this slaughtering control is in the interests of the packers, but the fact is that some slaughtering control is absolutely necessary to make the rationing of meat a
success. To show how far they go in some countries, I would point out that in Great Britain they reduced the number of slaughtering places by ninety-five per cent.
Yes; but they have not the distances that we have in Canada. It is altogether different over there. The whole country could be put in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We do not go to anything
like the lengths they have gone over there.

Might I ask a question at
this point about the construction of the new wartime prices and trade board temporary building in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Did the minister consider
the advisability of the erection of this building?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I did.

In the minister's opinion, in view of the fact such a tremendous amount of lumber and materials are required for construction, might not some alternative plan have been arrived at, rather than use up all these valuable materials and man-power. Was the situation thoroughly canvassed as to whether or not these various parts of the board could not have been left where they were, or put in other places, either in Ottawa or in adjoining cities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member has no conception of how thoroughly that situation was canvassed. I can say it was canvassed very thoroughly. The wartime prices and trade board was at that time in twenty-two separate places in Ottawa. They were spread around throughout the city. We were trying our best to send as many branches or divisions out of the city as we could. For instance, the rationing administration, with a tremendous personnel, is established in Montreal. But we can go only so far in that direction. It was expensive and it was inefficient. It was a. waste of time, money and everything else to operate in that way, to have one administration here and another there. I came to the conclusion it was necessary to have these branches together, under one roof, if possible.
Then the question was raised: Where? That was discussed very thoroughly. The proposal eventually adopted is by far the cheapest of the alternative proposals considered-and several were considered.
