Mr. O'NEILL: Is the slaughtering of hogs on the quota basis in British Columbia, and are the accredited' abattoirs under the control of the packers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The quota that can be slaughtered is fixed by the meat board, formerly known as the bacon board. Is the hon. member talking about hogs alone, or does he include beef as well?
Mr. O'NEILL: When the slaughtering of beef animals was first considered it was put on a quota basis. That is to say, if a certain company slaughtered a thousand animals last year they were permitted to slaughter whatever percentage is allowed them this year. Eor instance, if it were ninety per cent, then they would be permitted to slaughter 900 animals.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. O'NEILL: But that system was abandoned. At the present time while there is a quota, that quota is not divided among the packers on the same basis as it was last year. They are allowed to slaughter so many cattle. But there is no certain quota fixed for any one company. I was wondering if the same thing now applies to hogs, or whether each packer is allowed a certain quota of hogs to slaughter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a quota for each slaughtering place. For export houses the quota is fifty per cent of 1940, and for others it is seventy-five per cent of 1941. That is fixed by the meat board.
Mr. O'NEILL:	What about domestic
consumption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The export houses have for their domestic quota fifty per cent of 1940; and the others-those which are not export establishments-have seventy-five per cent of 1941.
Mr. O'NEILL: Are the accredited slaughtering abattoirs under the control of the packers, or are there independent slaughtering houses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There have been 12,000
slaughter permits issued, and there are about forty-five or fifty inspected houses. I cannot imagine that all of them are controlled or owned by the packing industry. I do not think that would be the case at all.
Mr. O'NEILL: I understand that there are only three in Vancouver, two of which are owned and controlled by Canada Packers, Swifts or some of the others, the third one being an independent house. However, I understand that negotiations are under way by

the packing concerns to get hold of this house. The government will not permit animals to be slaughtered except in an accredited slaughter house. If the packers own all these places, there will be no place for an independent man to slaughter his stock. The independent man always pays the producer anywhere from two to three cents a pound more than the packer pays. I shoidd like to have this matter cleared up, because it is of great concern to producers in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall have to get some information for the hon. gentleman. I did not understand that he was asking a question; I thought he was just making a statement. I shall look into the situation.
The minister will see how the small producer is gradually being squeezed out of existence.

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to a particular situation which arises in the lower part of the Gaspe coast where the only means of transport is by water. It may happen that during the season of navigation a merchant may not get in sufficient sugar, syrup and other foodstuffs to last thoughout the winter, and the result is that before spring the population is short of these items. Last fall they could not secure sufficient molasses and sugar to-last until the spring. Since last spring some of the ships which used to carry on this trade have been sold to other companies and it is not expected that they will be kept on this route. We are afraid that sufficient stocks of food will not be brought in before the fall to last until next spring. I suggest to the minister that this board should make sure that necessary stocks are delivered to last throughout the winter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the responsibility of the wartime prices and trade board to attend to the proper distribution of foodstuffs to meet a situation of that kind. I understand that the local merchant makes arrangements for delivery of what he requires, and if he anticipates any difficulty it is open to him to apply to the wartime prices and trade board.

Will the minister make sure
that the board investigates the matter and sees to it that sufficient supplies are taken in before toe close of navigation? Orders should be given to the board to proceed with this investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are fully aware of their responsibility in that regard. In view of the fact that the hon. member has publicly called attention to the necessity of seeing that trans-

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
portation is provided, I am sure that they will give attention to this matter. I shall suggest to them that they do.

Before I ask some questions that I have in mind I should like to say a word of praise to the minister. I am sure he has not expected this of me. I understand in our neighbouring country to the south they have had to make three changes in the gentlemen who have been in charge of their price control. I congratulate the minister upon being so successful in securing the man he did. I disagree ninety per cent with what he says, but I believe he has the courage of his convictions. He has stayed with what he started out to do. However, I would say that I do not think this gentleman has the foggiest notion of what he is talking about in connection with agriculture.
The first question I have to ask is in connection with an order for return brought down on July 1. This contained a number of questions in connection with sugar, but the fifth question asked if women's organizations had been represented at the negotiations that were carried on and, if so, which ones? I know the minister will not have these answers with him, so that I shall give the answer that was given. The answer was that the foods administration, the ration administration, the consumer branch of the wartime prices and trade board and the consumer branch of the Department of Agriculture each had a woman representative attending these discussions. I should like to know who- these ladies were, who appointed them and what organizations were represented.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The lady representing the consumer branch of the wartime prices and trade board was Miss Sanders. The consumer branch is a voluntary organization of the women of Canada, consisting of about
12.000	in all. The lady from the foods admin>-istration was Miss Speers, a nutrition expert and a member of the staff of that administration. The lady representing the Department of Agriculture was Miss Pepper, and the lady representing the ration administration was Miss Archer.

On July 6 I asked this question:
Will salmon be released- and distributed for Canadian consumption on a per capita basis to each province?
I was informed in reply that approximately
200.000	cases of canned salmon will be released for Canadian consumption but that the basis of distribution had not been determined. I also asked further questions in reference to canned herring on the same day. The reason
I asked those questions was that my information was that last year herring from the Atlantic coast was distributed in British Columbia while all the herring in that province went to the British market. I think the public are entitled to know the answers to the questions, and I must say that I do not particularly appreciate the answers that were given me. I will give the questions and answers:
3.	Will canned herring be released for distribution to the several provinces?
The answer to that was:
3.	Certain quantities of canned herring are being considered for Canadian consumption but the basis of distribution cannot be determined until the quantity to be available is known.
Then I asked:
4.	If so, on what basis?
The answer to that was:
4.	See answer to question 3.
Then question 5 was:
5.	Will eastern herring be shipped to British Columbia ?
The answer to that was:
5.	See answer to question 3.
My last question was:
6.	Will British Columbia canned herring be released on the Pacific coast?
The answer to that was:
6.	See answer to question 3.
British Columbia produces as much fish as any other seven provinces in the Dominion, and my question now is, do the wartime prices and trade board, in their so-called maintaining of the price ceiling and of the so-called cost of living index, believe that herring from the Atlantic coast can be transported to British Columbia, where we produce as much fish as any other seven provinces-those are the figures of the bureau of statistics-and sold *there, while our herring in British Columbia is taken overseas and the so-called cost of living index be maintained under .those circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I understand it, nothing is settled about the distribution of herring this year. I think the answer to question No. 5 which my bon. friend has just quoted indicates that nothing is settled. The answer means nothing much more than that the matter is under consideration. The hon. gentleman is complaining that last year some herring from the eastern coast was sent to British Columbia, while British Columbia herring was sent to Britain. I do not know the facts of the case. Perhaps my colleague the Minister of
4470	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
Fisheries has something to do with the distribution of the fish production of this country. I do not know whether he will be able to throw any light on that.

With all due deference to the minister, and I have given credit where credit is due, I do not agree with the cost of living index, and I am doing my best to point out that the figures are not true, when herring from the Atlantic coast can be moved to British Columbia whose fish production is the equivalent of any other seven provinces. My interpretation of the answers that were brought down in reply to my questions is that the wartime prices and trade board-not the Department of Fisheries-determines how and where the fish is to be distributed. I should like to be corrected if I am wrong. May I ask the minister whether fish from the Atlantic coast are to be released for local consumuption on the eastern seaboard, and whether fish from the western coast will be released to that district?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matter is not determined yet. The answers to the questions show that. I rather intimated a moment ago that perhaps the Department of Fisheries has the distribution or allocation of fish under its control. That is not so. The wartime prices and trade board looks after .the distribution of fish in Canada, while the Department of Fisheries takes responsibility for the export of fish. The allocation or distribution of fish to meet the demands of the Canadian market is the responsibility of the wartime prices and trade board. What arrangements will be made for the present year remains to be seen. That has not yet been determined.

I have another
matter to take up with the minister. I have already taken it up with 'his parliamentary assistant. My information is that on June 21 a firm of canners in British Columbia received a call from the office of the wartime prices and trade board in Victoria that the Department of Munitions and Supply would call for the release of 5,000 pounds of jam for a boat, presumably a naval boat. It is not in the public interest to make the name public. This firm of canners replied that they did not have available that quantity of free stocks, but that they had it in frozen stocks. They were informed that they could not release that amount from the frozen stocks, but that they could from the free stocks, but that if munitions and supply had Ottawa requisition the wartime prices and trade board it could be done. I was informed that that was entirely incorrect. That was the answer given by the department, under date of July 2, at Mission,

British Columbia. On the morning of the 21st of June a telephone call was received from the wartime prices and trade board that munitions and supply office at Victoria would be telephoning and asking for 5,000 pounds of jam, and that United Farmers Cooperative Exchange could supply them out of free stocks but not out of frozen. According to the statement of the manager, in his letter, the board stated that-
. . . we could supply them out of our free stocks but not to send any out of the "frozen" stocks-we had 1,600 cases of frozen jam in our warehouse at the time. I said we were sold out of free stocks, which they already knew.
This is the important part:
I asked for the release of 100 cases of 4-lb. jam if they phoned for it but the answer I got was that they had no. power in Vancouver to release any frozen jam to the naval stores at Victoria.
Shortly afterwards another telephone call came from Victoria asking if the firm could ship 5,000 pounds of jam to the naval stores at Esquimalt. In case any hon. members from the Atlantic coast do not know, Esquimalt is the foundation of the entire defence of the Dominion of Canada on the Pacific coast; it is our Halifax, only a far greater port. I do not want to weary the committee by reading the whole letter.
You are bragging.

Maybe I am bragging. I am entitled to brag about my province. But there is something wrong, to my mind, when naval stores cannot get a release of jam at any time without having to go through all this rigmarole.
Here is the point which I am most concerned about. The wartime prices and trade board have-I say this with all due deference- no greater influence than possibly their master the Canadian Manufacturers' association. This firm got in touch with the Canadian Manufacturers' association, and they immediately took the matter up. I should be glad to give the minister a copy of this letter. They informed the firm that they could do nothing about the matter. But then, as this boat had to leave, the firm shipped the jam on their own responsibility. The wartime prices and trade board called them up and severely bawled them out. They had forwarded requisition order No. C-1382.
And never got the jam?

And never got the
jam? That I do not know. The point I am trying to get at is this. Are a few officials here, who do not even know there is a war

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
on, to have the privilege of denying our navy jam when requisition is made in due order, and then afterwards it is O.K'd with a number I have given, requisition order C-1382? This can be checked from the records-the Oii'ing of the order. What I am interested in knowing is this, can the Department of Munitions and Supply at any time requisition jam or any other food product for our armed forces without being hindered by the wartime prices and trade board?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
As my hon. friend indicated, I took this matter up when he first put his inquiry before me. The inquiry took the form of a statement that he had been informed that a firm in Vancouver, United Farmers Cooperative, had been refused permission to deliver frozen stocks of jam to the Department of Munitions and Supply, presumably for the armed forces. I took the matter up with the wartime prices and trade board; and I was informed that, while frozen stocks of jam were, of course, under the control of the wartime prices and trade board, on no occasion had they refused a requisition from the Department of Munitions and Supply for the armed forces. In addition, that morning they telephoned long distance to the wartime prices and trade board office in Vancouver and were informed by the office in Vancouver that they had received no request from United Farmers Cooperative for delivery of jam to munitions and supply. I communicated that information to my hon. friend, and that is the last I heard of it until to-night. If the jam supplies were required for the navy, as I take it from what he said they were, as the committee knows purchases for any of the armed forces are made through munitions and supply. But the point I wish to make is that the wartime prices and trade board food administration stated without qualification that they had never refused a request from the Department of Munitions and Supply for frozen jams or any other food products, and that in the case of this particular company they had been informed over the long distance telephone, on inquiring, that no request for delivery had been received.
There may have been some mix-up in the filing of the requisition-I do not know as to that-but that is the information which the board here were given by their office in Vancouver. If my hon. friend has any further particulars, we shall be glad to go into the matter and see what happens.
Mr. CRUICKSHANIv:	I thank the parliamentary assistant. I am not quarrelling with him; he gave me a very fair report 72537-283
at the time and answered every question I asked. This firm may be wrong in their information, but they are the largest independent jam firm in the Dominion of Canada

I repeat that, "independent jam firm in the Dominion of Canada"-and they make the definite statement that they were turned down on this. Eveiybody knows that no firm has any difficulty in selling this kind of produce. The firm are not worried about the order; but what I am interested in and what the manager of the firm is interested in and took upon himself as a good Canadian to bring to my attention, is that some naval boat-I reiterate, what we hear so often, that "it is not in the public interest" to say what particular boat, because apparently anything we do not want to mention is not in the public interest-required this jam, could not get it, and he took it upon himself to release this jam. I want to know whether the wartime prices and trade board, either any official or the whole board, has any power to refuse to release jam or any other food to any branch of the armed forces. I am entitled to an answer to that question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Just to answer my hon.
friend's last point, these frozen stocks to which he is referring, of jam and other products, are frozen, not because the wartime prices and trade board wants to freeze them, but at the request of the Department of Munitions and Supply in order that they may be sure that there will be an adequate supply for the armed forces. As I say, it is possible that in this case naval stores or some group like that attempted to order this jam direct from the supplier without going through munitions and supply. I cannot say as to that. But the important point in principle is that the wartime prices and trade board does not refuse and has not refused requisitions from munitions and supply for the armed forces, and the purpose of freezing these stocks is at the request of munitions and supply in order that they will be available for the armed forces.
Mr. O'NEILL:	I did not know that my
hon. friend was going to switch from salmon to jam, or I would have risen before. I wish to ask a question with respect to salmon. My understanding is that 200,000 cases of salmon will be released for domestic consumption. Can the minister say whether it will be released on the percentage of population of the different provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The basis of distribution
has not been settled. Discussions covering

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
the whole distribution of fish are going on between the board and the Department of Fisheries at the present time.
Mr. O'NEILL:	Would it be unfair to
have it allocated on a percentage basis of the population? ,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not see anything unfair about it, if everything else is allocated on that basis. Whether it was fair or not might depend upon the allocation of other foods.
Mr. O'NEILL:	I should now like to ask
a question with respect to jam. Is more jam being released to the German internment camps than is being allocated to the civilian population of this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The German prisoners get the same rations as -the depot troops in Canada. That is by virtue of the Geneva convention. How that compares with the amount available for the civilian population I do not know. It it not a ration to the civilian population. One would have to know how much is available and find how much that would give to every civilian in Canada and compare the result with the army ration. That is what it amounts to.
Mr. O'NEILL: I am not very familiar with the matter, and possibly the minister does not buy any more tins of jam off the shelves in the stores than I do, but I understand from my wife that there are many days when there is no jam on the shelves, though occasionally you will find it in the stores. Yet there is common gossip that there is all the jam in the German camps that they require.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There has been a large increase in the amount of jam available for the civilian population of Canada, but even a greater increase in the demand. A good instance of this will be found in the statement I made when the wartime prices and trade board1 estimates were introduced. I quote from page 4256 of Hansard.	y
A good instance of this is jams, jellies and marmalades. Before the war the production of these items w-as in the neighbourhood of 45 million pounds. _ By 1942 the output had risen to over 70 million pounds. Of this total some 15 million pounds were used by the armed forces and other priority users, but there still remained a considerably larger quantity for civilians. Yet hon. members, or at least their wives, know that jams, jellies and marmalades are very difficult to obtain in retail stores.
It shows the increase in the supply and the greater increase in the demand for jams, jellies and marmalades.

I wish the minister would clarify the Canadian War Orders and Regulations, Ottawa, June 28, 1943. There is

one point that I do not understand. Let me quote from order No. 289, respecting maximum manufacturers' prices of certain groceries. I quote:
The board hereby orders as follows:-
1.	The schedule to order No. 116 of the board is hereby amended by deleting therefrom the words "jam, jelly and marmalade" and substituting therefor the word "marmalade".
The second paragraph is the one I do not understand:
2.	The said schedule is hereby further amended by deleting therefrom the words "clothes pins".
Would the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was a special order, with ,a long list of articles sold by grocery stores, including clothes pins, and they therefore appeared in the schedule. One by one specific orders were made relating to the prices of these articles. I do not know whether all or even most of them have been covered, but at any rate clothes pins are among those that have been.' When a specific order was made the article affected ceased to be subject to the general order and therefore was taken out of that general order by deletion from the schedule.
It has nothing to do with jams?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. Jams appear elsewhere on the list.

I think the minister made a timely statement this evening. It is one that should have been made some time ago. It dealt with the many difficulties which the board has and the manner in which it is trying to cope with the various problems. A good deal of information was given us to-night which I think is worth while, and I endorse the suggestion made by the hon. member for Swift Current, that the statement given to-night should be summarized and set out in concise form by a certain representative of the press whom he mentioned and who would be capable of doing it. He suggested that it be published in the weekly newspapers so that the people would have -the information. I am prompted to support that suggestion by tire statement made by the hon, member for Saskatoon. He indicated- some of the difficulties which merchants, consumers and others have through failure to understand the working of the prices board and also the changes in prices. The local merchants in my own district face these difficulties. I have heard them complain- that there is so much confusion and lack of understanding in the method of carrying out the different regulations, and of the changes in -prices. As the

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
hon. member for Saskatoon said, the information sometimes gets out in advance, while in other cases there is delay, I have heard both consumers and local merchants complain. I will not enlarge on this, though I have letters which I could read toi illustrate what I am saying. However, I am trying to be brief. I suggest that the statement be summarized and given out. Yesterday there was some discussion on the question of rent and rent control and prosecutions, and in that regard I have had some complaints.
The hon. member for Haldimand suggested this afternoon that the producers should have had representation on the prices board. On page 73 of the report referred to yesterday by the minister we find a list of the board and the different firms whom they represent, but we do not see a real representative of producers there, apart from the Department of Agriculture. I wish to endorse the statement made this afternoon by the hon. member fo.r Haldimand that we should have a real representative of the producers on this board. In my opinion we would have avoided many of the difficulties in regard to the ceiling on farm products if this had been done. I agree with the hon. member that ceiling prices on certain farm prodiicts are not fair or as close to parity prices as they should be.
To come back to the question of rentals, it was stated yesterday that during the nine months' period ending March 31 last there were 1,679 prosecutions, of which 730 corn cerned rentals. Would the minister give us a break-down of that figure of 730, to show how many of these prosecutions occurred in the western provinces? I hear many landlords in the city of Regina complaining about the enforcement of the rental regulations. I happen to have a block also and I could recite some of my own difficulties, but I shall not do so. It would satisfy me if the minister would say a word in regard to the prosecutions in the city of Regina. I hope the minister also will consider the suggestion advanced by the hon, member for Swift Current, which I am making on my own behalf now, that the public generally should have some better understanding as to how these matters are being regulated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am glad the making of the statement in regard to the cost of living index appears to have met with the approval of the committee. Personally I thought that even though it might take a little time it would be advisable to make a full statement on the matter because of its importance and the interest it has attracted, and I shall try
to see that the statement is given the widest possible circulation by the most efficient means.
With regard to the composition of the wartime prices and trade board and the suggestion that the farmers should be represented on it, as I have pointed out before, this board does not consist of representatives of any occupations at all; it consists entirely of senior government officials. On it there are two representatives of the Department of Agriculture, but it does not have representatives of any industry or occupation or calling. We have kept it strictly to government officials, because it is not a gathering place for persons who represent their own points of view or the points of view of various groups-

I appreciate that, but it is
not any personal point of view I have in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not have before me
the information with regard to the rentals prosecutions by provinces, but I can get that information.

There is one
matter I should like to place before the minister, because I think it is of interest to every small retailer from the Atlantic to the Pacific. During the last few months there has been a marked trend toward a diminution in the numbers of small retailers throughout the dominion which, unless something is done to correct it, will ultimately lead to their general extinction. The reason for the failure of the small business man lies in the fact that he is unable to secure his fair and proper share of the consumer goods that remain to be distributed throughout the country as a whole. I hear this point raised on numberless occasions. It is said' that unless something is done very soon to put a halt to this trend, by the time the war is over the small retailer will be forced out of existence, to all intents and purposes, while on the other side of the equation we shall see an ever-increasing concentration in the hands of the large retail concerns throughout Canada.
I think every hon. member will agree that no group has done more for this country, in the remote settlements as well as in the more thickly populated parts, than the small merchant. We now have rationing of many of the necessities of life; we have rationing of gasoline, all under a body which has a large number of officials, and I should like to know what is being done to see that the small retailer obtains his fair and proper share of the consumer goods still available for distribution throughout the country as a whole.
4474	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
What is the scheme? What is being done to see that the various foods, the various kinds of clothing, and so on, are made available to the small retail stores which, after all, are the backbone of the business life of this country? What is being done by the wartime prices and trade board to see that these small businesses are treated fairly? This is a matter which deserves a complete answer on the part of the minister. As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has said, the statement made this evening by the minister about the operation of the index number with respect to the cost of living will do much to clear up the misunderstandings that one hears expressed on every hand. The consumer, too, has an interest in the small retail store, and to-day consumers complain that they are placed in the position that in many cases they can lo longer go to their local stores, because those stores do not have the goods available.
Just in that connection I wish to mention a matter which I think should be brought to the attention of the committee, for it illustrates in concrete form the tendency to give preference to large stores as opposed to the smaller stores. Following the rationing of tea, an order went out as late %s September, 1942, with respect to the distribution of tea in the northern parts of Canada. Here is the strange thing about the order which was made. The Indians were made subject to the rationing of tea, provided they did not deal with a certain well-known company which operates in the north. If they were dealing with this very large corporation operating in northern Canada they were not required to have ration coupons.

What company was
that?

The Hudson's Bay company. If, on the other hand, they wanted to deal with the small, independent trader, they could not do it without ration cards. What was the result of that order? I do not know whether it is in effect today, but it was in effect as late as October, 1942, and it was admitted to be in effect by Mr. George Short, director of commercial and institutional rationing. The effect was that when the Indians came in to buy their supplies, if they had no ration coupons and they went to the company's store they were able to purchase anything else they wanted. If they went to the independent trader, that was denied them. They would not buy the rest of their supplies because they could not secure their tea.
That is an order which I find difficult to understand. It had the effect of arousing the
lMr. Diefcnbaker.]
antagonism of all the smaller traders in the north, those men who carry on trade from the Hudson bay to the Yukon territory. It is an order which is unfair add unjustified. An explanation was given that any Indians who wished to buy from independent merchants may be directed to the nearest Indian agency for a requisition enabling them to buy from such independent merchant. That order. I submit, is one that cannot be justified.
I point this out for the purpose of indicating that there is a feeling that sufficient consideration is not being given by the government, through the instrumentality of the board, to the welfare of the small business people. For them I make this plea, and I ask that machinery be set up in addition to that already existing, which will assure to the small business man and the small retailer a fair and proper share of consumer goods, reduced as they are to-day in amount, by the exigencies of war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This subject probably
deserves a fuller explanation than I am prepared to give to-night. But I do not wish to go away and take the time to prepare a set speech or statement on it. I want to deal with it now, because it is the favourite procedure of certain critics of the wartime prices and trade board to state that the small retailer is being sacrificed to the big one. That is a favourite criticism. It was hinted by the hon. member for York-Sunbury the other night.

I am asking that
it be answered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And I will answer it. I
wish to say this, that if it had not been for the wartime prices and trade board and its policy, and if it had not been for the policies which have been pursued, the small retailer would have been in a far worse position than he is in to-day. I wish to give the reasons for saying that.
AVhen goods in short supply are faced with higher war-time costs of distribution, suppliers tend to divert, if left to themselves, larger shares of supplies to preferred customers, and for various reasons-because of larger orders, because of the stronger financial position on an average, because of the ability of the preferred customer to pay higher prices, as the result of having higher individual ceilings in a great many cases, because of lower freight absorption, and because of other considerations favourable to the seller.
The board, in 1942, published a statement of policy, which appeared in the Canada Ganette, and which I think I shall have to put

II ar Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
on record. It will take a little time to read it into the record. But from the beginning, at least from the fall of 1941, when the ceiling policy *went into effect, the board made it quite clear that there would be as equitable a distribution of supplies to all retailers, both large and small, as could be effected. The basis of that distribution was a ratable distribution of goods in short supply to 1942 customers, in proportion to their purchases during 1941. It was recognized that no base period could be completely satisfactory, on the basis of quota between areas and between outlets, but 1941 seemed to be the most satisfactory basis available.
Representations have been made to me by the hon. member for Assiniboia who knows about conditions in that part of Saskatchewan, and he argues that in that area purchases, on account of economic conditions, were limited in 1941, and that therefore the application of that formula is unjust to that area, and presumably to certain other areas in Canada.
It may be that the formula has not allowed for the increase in purchasing power in that particular part of Saskatchewan, the increase in the relative prosperity of the people. It may be that it does not allow for that factor. Other considerations have, however, been allowed-not there, necessarily-but quotas in certain designated areas have been increased to allow for the marked increase in population caused by the war, and wholesale and retail trade administrators have given individual adjustments in cases of anomaly. But the equitable distribution policy applies only to unrationed goods. Normally, under rationing, other controls-for example, the coupon flow-back-meet the needs of the situation.
An analysis was made to find out the effect of what was happening to the independent stores, chain stores, and departmental and mail order stores, in respect of sales and in respect of inventories. There is a small table I should read, which was prepared from dominion bureau of statistics' figures. It shows the change in sales between December, 1941, and December, 1942. There was no increase in sales by the department and mail order stores between December, 1941, and December, 1942. Therefore the percentage of increase is zero.

What about the
amount of supplies they had on hand in each of said years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will come to that. I am dealing now with sales. For the general stores there was an increase of 1-7 per cent in sales in 1942 over sales in 1941. For independent stores there was an increase in sales of thirteen per cent in December, 1942, over the same month in 1941.
Now, what about the change in inventory as between those two months? For the departmental and mail order stores there was a reduction in inventory of nine per cent. For the chain stores there was a reduction in inventory of -6 per cent. For the independents there was a reduction in inventories of one per cent. I gave some figures with regard to failures and so on when I introduced my estimates, but I should like to quote now from a speech delivered by Mr. P. K. Heywood of the Canadian retail federation at the retailers' war-time conference held in Toronto on Tuesday, April 6, 1943. The Canadian retail federation is an association made up largely, if not entirely, of small retailers. The chairman appears to be Mr. P. K. Heywood and the secretary is Mr. George S. Hougham. This is what Mr. Heywood said in his speech:
The federation has received a large measure of recognition, both by the wartime prices and trade board and by other agencies of government and, I believe, will be increasingly consulted on the vexing problems that have to be faced in the days ahead.
Now let us look for a moment at the position in which we find ourselves to-day and take a brief glimpse into the future.
As is usual when any sudden changes are encountered, there are many predictions of disaster and the institution of price ceiling legislation was not without such predictions. What are the actual results? In the first place, most classes of retail business have experienced a boom in sales unequalled in modern times and all classes would have experienced a similar boom had the civilian economy been equal to the task of production while also producing for war. This we know was not possible and many lines of household appliances, hardware, tires and the entire automotive industry are, in varying degrees, casualties of this war in a civilian sense. But the total impact of the war on retailing as a whole has so far been chiefly psychological. Government regulations, merchandise deliveries and man-power shortages seemed to be enormous difficulties-but the fact remains that most stores have been doing pretty well and have had a good year in 1942, with satisfactory profits even after taxes.
Many predictions have been, made as to the fate of the small retailer-that his doom was sealed-that 20.000 would go out of business this year. Such publicity is most unfortunate. Even in normal times over 12,000 retailers go out of business per annum but in normal times about an equal number start in business so the total remains about the same. During the present emergency none are starting in business and many more are going out because they can find more lucrative employment in other industries. The number of empty stores appearing in most cities is not nearly as serious as it might appear.
How many went out of business in 1942?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have no accurate figures on that.

Leader of the Official Opposition
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would gather from that, tha.t the store with more than two outlets and a central warehouse is treated as a wholesaler and gets the wholesale price instead of the retail price.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The wording of the order itself denies that argument because it says:
One-half cent per pound on purchases from him by a retailer.
That is on purchases by a retailer, not by a wholesaler, who operates more than two retail places of business and has a central warehouse for such place of business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And a central warehouse, it says. It is quite usual for chain stores to be treated as wholesalers in the pricefixing system of the country. They discharge the functions of wholesalers. They have their own warehouse and distribute the goods among their branches, and therefore it is quite usual for them to get a Lower price. They have higher charges because they do their own warehousing.
4478	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board

Do I understand that if the word "warehouse" were left out of the section, it would read differently. It is two distributing stores and a warehouse, and if the retailer does not operate the warehouse he does not get as large a discount.
M.r. GRAYDON: I would not mind continuing the argument if my hon. friend is going to get into it. As a matter of fact, we might as well be frank and say that the mark-up for the chain stores can be no greater than one-half a cent a pound. To be blunt, despite the explanation of the minister and the complementary remarks of the hon. member for Calgary West, the fact remains that the mark-up for any other retailer is 2J cents, and the arguments from time to time on this very point still stand, so far as I can see, despite the explanation which has been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It goes back to the old contention which used to be made, that the manufacturer should not charge any lower price to groups that did their own warehousing than to those who had no warehouse. That was all fought out in the price spreads committee, and there were different opinions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What was your view? You were on the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I forget about that, but I recognized, I think, the practice, which is practically universal and has been followed all through the years, of manufacturers giving a department store, a wholesaler, a chain store, and people who do their own warehousing or discharge the functions of a wholesaler a lower price than that at which they would sell direct to the retailer who did not discharge that function.

The interest of the minister is asked in a specific case of the administration of an order which not only results in hardship on the importer but is manifestly unjust. It will be recalled that in December last there was a broadcast, with some satisfaction to the corporation and with more satisfaction to the consumer, that oranges would be eligible for a subsidy, and the order was communicated to wholesalers. In the city of Trail there is a wholesale importing firm which does not resort to the railroads. Twice a week they go to the market in Spokane, which is the distributing centre for jobbers along the international boundary, and then they bring back their supplies, which, it will be readily seen, must be much fresher than those which come in the ordinary course by train. When this order came over the radio, the representative of the prices board resident

in Trail informed this particular wholesaler that he must reduce his price, which he did. He brought in three lots of oranges, and presented his application for his subsidy. Up to the time when the second lot was brought in, the representative of the board had not received any instructions as to the terms or conditions under which that subsidy would be granted, with the result that when the firm's application went in, the firm was told that the subsidy could not be paid to it for the reason that the application was not covered by the terms and conditions of the order of the board.
What was the firm to do? The representative had had no instructions; this firm acted in good faith, and the matter has been pending ever since last December, for the reason that the application was required to show, in order to cover the bonus, that these oranges were brought in, in carload lots, and that the importer had title at the source of production. What is a wholesaler on a small scale to do where he cannot afford to bring in carload lots? The nearest point to the interior where carload lots would be brought in would, I think, be Vancouver, 500 miles away, with two freights for the wholesaler to pay. This man complied with the principle of the order, which was to reduce the cost to the consumer. He has reduced the cost; he is out to the amount of his reduction on all three lots of oranges brought in, and yet up to to-day, notwithstanding the efforts of the representative of the prices board to secure an adjustment of the matter, that firm is still out of pocket. It is a small firm; it has been in operation for four years; its capital is limited, and it cannot very well stand the loss, nor can it afford to bring in oranges in carload lots.
It certainly means that communities in which there is not a large consumption must pay the old price and not have the benefit of the subsidy. I ask the minister if he does not think there is a direct injustice imposed, not only upon that importer, but upon the consumers in small communities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know anything about that case. I will take it up with the commodity prices stabilization corporation. I assume there is some explanation there. I have here a statement, though probably I had better not stop to read it, showing the treatment of oranges. We did not undertake to pay any subsidy, to start with, on oranges; we simply removed the duty; but later at some stage a subsidy was arranged for on carload shipments. I should not like to express any opinion about this case until I look it up in Hansard and bring it to the attention of the commodity prices stabilization cornnration. If

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
the hon. gentleman would like to take it up with them direct, I am sure that they would give him every courtesy and consideration in discussing it with him and dealing with it.
I should like to impress upon the minister that the department's own representative has not been able to get this adjustment, although he has been trying to do so ever since December.

I think all of us must congratulate the hon. member who has just taken his seat upon the clarity with which he presents his argument, depending as he does upon someone to read to him.
There are a number of questions I should like to'ask the minister, arising out of his statement. They are these:
In how many' cases has an order been made directing that a quota be given to a retailer who had complained that he was not receiving his proper share of'goods?
How many retail stores in Canada have been allowed to commence business since the order was made freezing the stores then in existence? I should like that information by provinces.
Also I would press upon the minister the necessity of answering the question I asked a while ago, namely, how many retail stores closed in the year 1942. Information must be available. The minister was able from the reading of a speech by one of the officials of the retailers' association to say that a certain number each year were expected to close up in the ordinary normal flow of business, and that usually that number was compensated for by the number of new businesses which opened up. That being so, the information must be available, and I would appreciate being informed as to how many retail stores have closed down. That answer will indicate whether or not there is anything to the argument that retail stores are greatly diminishing in number and importance throughout the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will get as much of that information as I can for the hon. gentleman and present it to-morrow.
The minister has said that no new business can be undertaken without a permit. If a man engaged in general hardware decides to take on household furnishings, would that not be permissible?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He cannot do that without a permit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the regulation with regard to the delivery of ice throughout the country? Is there a definite restriction, and to what extent does it apply?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Two or three weeks ago I made an announcement on that question. It was restricted to two deliveries a week-I speak from memory-and was extended by order of the board to six deliveries a week to residential customers. That order was to be effective from the 1st of June until the 1st of October.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The parliamentary assistant will find, I think, that it was originally three days a week, and not two, as he states.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes; it was three.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If it has been changed to six, there is no point in the question I was going to ask.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Shefford raised the question, and it was brought to the attention of the minister.

Since the rationing of meat, the retail butchers' stores have had a coupon bank in their local banks and they make purchases against the coupons banked with that institution. I am given to understand that in cutting up a carcase of beef there is anywhere from 75 to 100 pounds of waste. Has the board considered making an allowance for that waste to the retail butchers? If not, will consideration be given that matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My information is that the most detailed and careful consideration has been given and that a schedule of tolerances has been published.

I should like to have a statement from the minister with regard to the utilization of commodities which retail outlets are permitted to procure and which remain on their shelves for a considerable time. I come from an area where the lumbering industry is carried on extensively and where railroad ties, cordwood and so on are produced. I refer to the Rocky Mountain House area of Alberta. Rocky Mountain House itself serves a vast area and a tremendous industry, an industry producing commodities which are most essential to the prosecution of the war. They are having the most extreme difficulty in procuring equipment to carry on the industry. For example, they find it very difficult to obtain saws. The quota is ninety per cent less than pre-war stocks and their ability to produce is severely jeopardized. The board of trade of that town has communicated with me by resolution and by letter pointing out that there are communities of which they are aware which are securing ten per cent, as they are, of the pre-war quantities of such necessary tools, notwithstanding that the need does not exist for these tools in those communities. I

4480	COMMONS
War Appropriation

Finance-Prices Board
would assume from their letter that they are of the opinion that some check should be made upon these retail outlets, who are securing the allotment to which they are entitled but are not putting those commodities to use, though they are definitely required in some other area such as the one to which I have referred. What check is made upon the use of these tools that are allowed to go to these retail outlets?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The suggestion, as I understand it, is that these retailers get certain stocks which they do not need but to which they are entitled. Because they are entitled to a quota they get such stocks and keep them, though they do not sell them for some reason or another. Is that the suggestion?

Take Swede saws, for example, which are in popular demand in that area. In some areas you will see them on the retail shelf for a period of two years. The retailer procures them because he feels that he is entitled to a certain quota, but no purchaser comes to demand them, and he keeps them there. I say that a commodity such as a Swede saw, for which there is such a demand in the area that I have referred to, should be sold where it is needed. There should be some claim on that article where it is required, and the board should endeavour to see that such articles are placed where there is a shortage and where they will be made use of.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is some machinery for the exchange of dormant stocks. I do not know much about it, but I will get some information in that regard. I should be surprised if what the hon. member describes as a condition is a prevalent one, because the retailer does not have to take his quota, and he would hesitate before buying something in which his capital would be tied up for two or three years if he could not dispose of it.

In the hardware line that happens frequently. Stocks are carried for two or three years, especially if the dealer thinks it may become more difficult to procure such stocks in the months ahead. Be that as it may, let us take the situation at Rocky Mountain House, where commodities such as I have mentioned are produced. Since production is jeopardized-users having encountered a ninety per cent reduction in the volume of the tools that are necessary to their production-what should dealers do in order to have their quota increased? What would be the procedure for them to follow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They should apply to the
retail or wholesale trade administrator. If the stocks are available, there is jurisdiction under the order to increase quotas under certain circumstances. I would not give any undertaking that they would be increased, but that is the procedure to follow. There is a bulletin dated June 15, 1943, called the "Wholesalers' Bulletin," which gives instructions about this whole matter. One of the sections has to do with increased quotas for selected areas, and it has notes on alternative systems for distributing goods on the quota basis, and so on.
I keep undertaking to give information later on, and I want to carry out that undertaking. The hon. member for Mackenzie asked me this afternoon to say something about the truck distribution of soft drinks and beers. The purpose of the trucking restrictions is to secure economical and efficient transportation. Before the restrictions were put in force a very large part of the distribution of beer and soft drinks was handled by trucks. By a combination of the thirty-five mile limit and gasoline rationing, the reduction in the miles travelled has approximated sixty per cent. In the administration of the thirty-five mile limit, permits for 203 beer trucks and 222 soft drink trucks have -been granted in individual cases where the administration- was satisfied that it was efficient to do so. One factor taken into account in reviewing applications for permits is whether or not a full load will be carried on the round trip. Many trucks are loaded-only when making deliveries and are empty on the return trip. Soft drink and beer trucks normally carry a full return load of empty bottles. There are a great many factors to be considered in any particular case; but by way of illustration, rather than explanation, a number of permits have been granted to permit deliveries to army camps.
This afternoon the hon. member for Peterborough West read a letter which was sent by a wholesaler to a retail customer, if I understood it correctly, in which he purported to quote an order of the wartime prices and trade board to the effect that certain- kinds of cloth were to be used for making suits of clothes for members of the air force only and not for members of the other two services, and the hon. member asked for an explanation of that order. I have had inquiries made, but no one in the wartime prices and trade board seems to know anything about any such order. They have no record of it at all, so that I shall have to ask the hon. member to get a little more information. If he can direct me to the order; if he can give the number, or

War Appropriation-Finance-Prices Board
tell me who issued it, I shall trace it further, but it may be that the wholesaler in question made a mistake when, he said it was an order of the wartime prices and trade board.

Has the minister given consideration to making it possible under certain circumstances to cut a ration coupon in two? Sometimes they do not fit in properly, and. it has been suggested that it might be advisable to be able to split them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For what commodity?
I cannot say which one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The coupons have been worked down to call for a normal sized package. For instance, I should not think anyone would want to use half a tea coupon, since a tea coupon is good for only two ounces in any ease. In the same way, I do not think anyone would want to split a butter coupon.
What about meat?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, the weekly ration is split; there are two coupons a week.

This is what I mean. If you go into a store to buy a roast of beef and it comes to say, four and a half pounds, the butcher will ask you to take half a pound of bacon, or something like that, to fill out tlhe coupon. My observation is that sometimes you are tempted to buy something you really do not need.

I had two things in mind, and one of them was the point mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. The other is this. I would not advocate that a person should be permitted to use half a coupon by itself, but when you make a purchase of meat which requires two and a half coupons, either you buy more than you require or you buy something that you do not want. The only other alternative is to waste that half coupon. This was brought to mv attention, and it appeared to me that something might be done about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is just a question of how finely you should divide it. Certainly it would complicate the banking arrangements quite a lo,t to have a much larger number of pieces of paper. A great deal of thought has been given, to this subject.
Is anything being done with regard to the meat used for sausages and hamburg, which we discussed here some time ago?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I have a memorandum on that matter which I seem to have mislaid. 72537-284 J
A check was made at .the various regional offices of the board, and it was found that there was very little waste in connection with either sausages or hamburg. There were four or five areas, among them Ottawa and London, Ontario, which did report that in the first week or two there seemed to be a considerable surplus of sausages and perhaps some waste, but the genera! report throughout the country was that there was no abnormal waste.
Did that apply also to the meat going into hamburg?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.

A very thorough check was made by the officials of the Toronto district, and after canvassing the situation very carefully they were of opinion that the waste is nothing more than normal for this season of the year. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox raised a question to which the minister said he would give some consideration. I just want to place on record my view that the only proper way of handling this situation is that now employed, the method of allowing a tolerance. If we were to try to ration the waste, the task would be almost impossible, principally because the waste is not all in connection with one commodity. There are many varieties of waste, perhaps not all pertaining to the commodity for which the ration ticket was issued, and there would be no way of separating one kind of waste, coming from a rationed product, from another kind coming from a non-rationed product. So that if you tried to issue ration coupons for waste, you would have confusion worse confounded. You might better continue to control the situation by allowing a definite tolerance on the rationed article, rather than to try to issue coupons for the waste.

give any information with regard to the restrictions on the delivery of bread beyond the thirty-five mile limit, either by truck or by rail, from bakeries in cities and towns?

I have no information on
that matter with me at the moment. If this item goes through, I think I could give that information on the next item without doing any great violence to the rules.
